subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND PORTUGAL

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND PORTUGAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I wish to announce that the government of Canada and the government of Portugal have concluded am agreement for air services between their respective territories. This agreement, in the main, follows the form of previous bilateral civil aviation agreements which Canada has already concluded. It makes provision for an air line designated by each government to operate a return, service originating in its own territory and terminating in, or passing through, the territory of the other country, and includes an exchange of the first four freedoms.
The route to be operated by the designated air line of Canada is specified as Montreal via such intermediate stopping places as may be mutually agreed to the Azores and/or Lisbon, and thence to the United Kingdom and countries beyond in both directions. The route laid down for the designated Portuguese air line is from the Azores and/or Lisbon via such intermediate' stopping places as may be mutually agreed to Montreal and countries beyond in both directions.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce with respect to the proposed international wheat agreement. It arises out of a report emanating from London that "hopes for a world wheat pact were publicly blown sky high this week", and a further reference to the Canadian High Commissioner in London, Mr. Norman Robertson, who is reported as suggesting "that the meeting might be continued". The article concludes that it was finally decided to hand the corpse over to the international council in Washington for disposal. My question is this: Is it correct that the plans for an international wheat agreement have broken down? Also will the minister communicate to the house the substance of any report he may have received on the matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be only a fair statement to say that the quotation read by the hon, leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) is a gross exaggeration, and I might add that that- remark applies to much that has been appearing in editorials and in leading articles on editorial pages in recent months.
The actual facts are that conversations have been continuing for some time in London among officials and those conversations went as far as it was possible for the officials to carry them. It was decided to have the question further dealt with by the different governments concerned, and prior to that the international wheat council was asked to have further conversations. The representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce, Doctor Wilson, has just flown back from England and is meeting with the wheat committee of the cabinet some time today to make an oral report. I am not sure how soon it will be possible for me to make a definite report to the house.

Mr. Speaker, if I might be permitted a comment, I am glad to hear the minister say that these reports are exaggerated. I would suggest that in view of the importance of the matter the actual facts ought to be made available to the house and the public as soon as possible.

speechtext:
When the committee rose last night it was considering order in council P.C. 1997 having to do with timber regulations as amended.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): I wish to join with the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, who was supported by the hon. member for Rpyal in his remarks on the lumber situation in the maritime provinces. Coming as I do from Nova Scotia I am perhaps more familiar with the situation there-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Is the hon. member speaking for both members for Halifax?

Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
On this occasion I am happy to associate myself with the hon. member for Nova Scotia sitting on the government side and with the hon. member for Royal sitting on the side which is also occupied by my hon. friend.
I think I can safely say that in the over-all picture so far as controls affect the maritime lumber industry we have no great fault to find with them except from the standpoint of the export buisness. I can confidently state that the lumber industry in the maritimes is in a prosperous condition at the present time. I would not want the rest of Canada to think that we were not taking full advantage of the markets which have been provided for us. Both the export and the domestic markets have been good. The entire cut of the maritime provinces could not be permitted to be shipped overseas to our natural market, the United Kingdom, because of the need of lumber for construction purposes in our own country. That is generally understood, but at the same time I support the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg in his contention that there should be a larger quota for the export business.
A careful check of the lumber production figures for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick will show that the total sawn lumber for Nova Scotia in 1939 was 270 million feet, and for New Brunswick 150 million feet, or a total maritime production in 1939 of 420 million feet. In 1945 Nova Scotia showed a cut of 338 million feet and New Brunswick 295 million feet, or a total of 633 million feet for the two provinces. The year 1946 showed about the same figure, a total of 632 million feet. Therefore you will see, Mr. Chairman, that we have had an increase from 1939 to 1945 in our sawn lumber production of something like 50 per cent. Of the 632 million feet sawn in 1946, 270 million feet were permitted to be exported free of the quota, leaving in Canada the remainder, 362 million feet. With 362 million feet we believe that a further export permit should be granted, because our normal needs in the maritimes in pre-war days did not come up to anything like this requirement. I suggest that the minister should give very careful thought to a further quota so far as the maritimes are concerned. We in the maritimes are not like [DOT]Quebec and Ontario, blessed with a large number of industries. We depend to a great extent on farming, mining, lumbering and fishing, and it is because of our export business that we need this increased quota on lumber. Last year we were very fortunate, although
somewhat handicapped owing to lack of ships to carry lumber overseas. In fact, generally speaking, transportation difficulties tied up our operations to a very marked extent. This was unavoidable because of the weather conditions in Ontario and elsewhere throughout Canada, which kept back from the maritimes a large number of cars that would otherwise have been used for carrying lumber to the ports of Halifax and Saint John. Representations have been made by the maritime lumber export commission or association to the minister or to the controller on more than one occasion. A study of 1946 production and distribution figures reveals that 258 million feet was retained for use in the maritimes, and in seven pre-war years an average of approximately 90 million feet per year was required. That leaves a very wide gap, and without taking away from our domestic requirements there is a large quantity that could be added to our export quota, thus adding to the prosperity of the maritime provinces.
I need not point out that basically our lumber industry has been export. The United Kingdom has been a great market for many years and, as was brought out by the hon. member for Royal, we want to maintain that pre-war market. We are sending large shipments there and are supplying our lumber at a reasonable price. I would point out to the hon. member for Royal that his statement is not entirely correct as regards the price of maritime lumber. Our price to the United Kingdom is something like $15 to $20 per thousand cheaper than the lumber which is supplied to that market by Russia, Denmark and Finland, which are the only other countries selling to the United Kingdom. The controller and the minister would be well advised to take this matter into consideration when dealing with the question raised by the member for Queens-Lunenburg, when he asked for a larger quota.
We could very well increase our quota without hardship to our domestic market. I want to support the contention of one hon. member with regard to birchwood. Our birchwood today is in such a condition that unless we cut and sell it we shall not be able to supply any market, either domestic or export, in the course of a few years. I note, in the provincial report recently tabled, the forty-sixth report of the Department of Lands and Forests of Nova Scotia, that the minister directing that department states:
The unsatisfactory ceiling price of hardwood will affect hardwood production adversely. This
Emergency Powers

is particularly regrettable in view of the almost certain loss of all our merchantable birch within five years.
That is the birch to which I refer. I wish to emphasize that and to bring it to the attention of the minister because of the need of taking care of this particular growth. It will be a total loss unless opportunity is given Nova Scotia and the maritime interests generally to sell that wood on the export market.
It is interesting to note that last year we had an increased production in Nova Scotia of 8-35 per cent. Softwood long lumber was up 25 million feet board measure, while hardwood showed a slight decline. Throughout the year all wood products were in great demand, and there is every indication that a similar condition will exist throughout 1947. That is from the report of the department of lands and forests of Nova Scotia.
This matter was so thoroughly covered by hon. members who have already taken part in the debate that I do not think it is necessary to dwell on the importance of the minister giving consideration to the lumber industry from the standpoint of the maritimes. It is estimated that about 78 per cent of New Brunswick and 68 per cent of Nova Scotia is still forested. The newsprint mills in four New Brunswick towns and in Liverpool, Nova Scotia, the Mersey mill-produce eight per cent of the total Canadian capacity. Most of that hardwood lumber is used locally, because the high cost of transportation to central Canada and the tariff that keeps it out of New England have to be reckoned with. It is because of these two factors, high transportation cost to central Canada and the more or less high tariff into New England, that I urge the minister to give every opportunity to the promotion of the export trade.
The present position on distribution is that United Kingdom quota has been filled. The forty million free quota has been distributed and the lumber placed by the shippers. There is a definite weakening in the eastern United States market and local demand has not increased. It is surprising to me that the local market has not increased, in view of the large amount of construction work going on in our province. I remember hearing recently something said by a gentleman who had been motoring from New York to Halifax. He said that as he drove through Massachusetts and the state of Maine he noticed very little construction work going on. When he came into New Brunswick there were signs of increasing construction of houses, but when he struck the Nova Scotia border there was an almost continuous line of houses being constructed for

veterans and others. I thought that was a very good tribute to the manner in which those interested in Nova Scotia were carrying on construction, and notwithstanding the picture of blue ruin which has been painted by many members opposite in regard to construction work in other parts of Canada, we in Nova Scotia are carrying on in an aggressive manner. Nevertheless there is still a sufficient amount of lumber to permit increasing the quota for export business.
May I say a word about price. The hon. member for Royal raised this question, and he had reference to retail price. He was justified in bringing the matter to the attention of the committee. While the export business is sufficiently large-two to one-to take care of losses that may be sustained by those engaged in selling lumber on the domestic market, I do not think it is sound business that one should have to carry the other, and I suggest again that this question of retail prices, so far as the maritimes are concerned, be reviewed, as suggested by the member for Royal, to bring about a higher price so as to kill the black market if one exists. I do not think the black market is as large, as prosperous or as thriving as some would like to make it appear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is extensive.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Royal says it is extensive. If that is so in New Brunswick, I doubt very much if it exists to the same extent in Nova Scotia, but I am not going to argue the point. I will agree with him in regard to the raising of retail prices in order to make it possible to carry on in such a way that retailers will not have to operate at a loss.
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg should be complimented for bringing this question up at this time. I trust that the minister will give to the points raised his serious attention and not only perhaps allow those in the maritimes to export a larger quantity, but also give consideration to the retail price.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
As I come from a district which has a very large industry in timber and lumbering, I wish to say a few words, but I shall not detain the committee for more than four or five minutes. I remember the olden days in the city of Toronto, when almost everybody owned his own home, the lumbering industry, wholesale and retail, was one of the most important ones we had at the time, when the forests in northern Ontario and many other parts were cleared. Wood was also extensively used in stoves before the production of coal became a commercial industry. I

Emergency Powers
am not here to criticize anybody about the timber regulations or about what was done in peace or war, but I believe the government would be well advised to come to the help of this great industry.
I should like to see the priorities system abolished. I think it would aid housing if everybody had a chance, according to the law of supply and demand, to get the lumber of all kinds which they need to build houses. Now you find that houses are not being built but there are certain priorities which exist for certain corporations, many of which are controlled by the crown-there are priorities of all kinds-and even they are hard up sometimes for labour and materials. Rents of crown houses are reaching the point where they are too high for the ordinary workingman.
This industry has been one of the most important means of providing employment in Ontario. I should like to see the regulations eased very materially and the priorities eliminated as soon as the government can see fit to do that. In the first place, the housing situation is one of the most serious we have in our cities. Last night reference was made to it by the hon. member for High Park. There was a return made in response to a motion of mine about a certain number of buildings and sheds for the R.C.A.F. on the Toronto waterfront east of Yonge street, on the harbour land, which were erected during the war mainly for storage and other air equipment purposes. There was a return presented on July 4 last, sessional paper 187A. It shows that the cost of erecting sheds for the use of Royal Canadian Air Force on the Toronto waterfront was $1,355,028.86. The second question was:
2. What department of government had charge of the construction?
The answer was:
Plans and specifications were provided by the R.C.A.F. Contract was awarded by the Department of Reconstruction and Supply.
Workmen were then brought in-carpenters, bricklayers and others-and they came from all over Canada. We are going to have a serious situation in Ontario if they keep making it the headquarters for everybody who is out of work, except the ambassadors who are on the seven seas. These people were brought in from all over Canada to build these sheds when there was very serious unemployment in our city. What became of the sheds? They could have been used for housing. I have been in some of these Sheds. Some of those occupied by the officers were luxurious; I have never seen anything like them. Big sheds were erected on a large part of the
grounds from Yonge street down to Sherbourne street. The lands on which the sheds were erected were drained, and had storm sewers. They are right on Toronto's waterfront, on land donated by the city, east of where the boats come in and out on Toronto bay. They could have been used for housing purposes, but that was not done. It was not the fault of the city of Toronto.
I shall read the next questions:
4.	Have any been torn down or sold? If so, how many, to whom and at what price?
5.	Was any application received for use of these buildings to relieve the housing shortage? If so, from whom?
6.	What use has been made of these buildings (a) during the war; (b) afterwards?
The reply is that some of these sheds were sold to crown assets allocations committee and transferred to War Assets Corporation for disposal. I know that when a war is on, a war of greater magnitude than any other in history, mistakes will doubtless be made. We may expect that. We have them in peace, and we may expect them in war. The reply states that twenty-one of these buildings out of the sixty-five declared surplus to the War Assets Corporation have been demolished, and it is planned to tear down another twenty-eight. Of the remaining sixteen, nine have been sold as follows, and negotiations for the sale of the other seven are being proceeded with: two buildings sold to G. M. Graton and Company for $650 each, for removal. The lumber in them is worth more than that. It could have been used to build small houses. All kinds of doors, sash and windows were in them, which were made of some of the finest dressed lumber. Two buildings were sold to Toronto Home Missions Council for $650 each, for removal. One building was sold to Centre Island Association, Toronto for S650, for removal. One building was sold to Mimico Rotaiy Club for $535, for removal. There were three buildings sold to the Toronto Star for $5,160. I had better be careful because there is a libel suit on. I do not know whether that is a "5" or a "3", but it looks like a "5". I have no qualified privilege, or any privileges at all, because, according to one morning newspaper columnist the members of parliament do not do anything at all. We might as well all go home, according to one of the columnists. I am not here to criticize them, because you can never answer newspapers. They always have the last word. I found that out years ago as the humble head of the city. We all make mistakes as well as the newspapers.
Emergency Powers

I find here that three buildings were sold to the Toronto Star for $5,160. The note here is tihat "in the first four above sales the prices took into consideration the fact that purchasers had to remove the buildings from the site and restore the land to its original condition at their own expense". My first point is that the lumber could have been used for small housing; my second point is that the buildings could have been used where they were for emergency housing. * There was water, light and overflow sewers. These buildings could have been used and could have been occupied by a very large number of people for emergency and trailer housing. I would point to the buildings down by the Toronto baseball park at the foot of Bathurst street, Little Norway. Those buildings are not as well constructed; they did not have light or many other conveniences.
That is all I have to say about it. I do not know whether mistakes were made, but I believe that the lumber could have been used. We could have used the property to relieve the emergency housing situation among those who cannot enter their own houses. I am not saying that as criticism of anybody, but just making reference to it.
I would like to see something done. Who are getting this timber and this lumber? How is it the large banks are able to build skyscrapers, two of which are going up on King street in Toronto? They can get steel, lumber and everything they need. According to the Bank Act, banks may build only according to the size of the business they carry on, and they are not allowed to go into real estate; but today some of them are building 30- or 35- storey buildings. One bank building is being torn down, at the corner of King and Bay while another is going up. Where are they getting all the materials, when these buildings are not needed at all and while houses are so urgently required?
I do not think the banks belong to any benevolent society, as some people would like us to believe. They are not going to take in the soldiers and rent them living space on the top floors of their buildings. Far from it; they are going to rent that office space commercially and charge high prices for it, as they do with most of their properties.
Theatres are being built all over the city, as the hon. member for Davenport mentioned last evening. These people must have considerable influence down here at Ottawa. The members of this house are just ciphers, we were told in one of the newspapers the other day, but the people who own these theatres must be more than ciphers. They are the people behind the scenes, as someone used to 
call them-stuff-shirted nobodies. They come around this building and seem to have a great deal of influence no matter what government is in power. I do not see why these buildings are being constructed. In addition, different conventions come along and use up a lot of lumber and other building material. Our schools are crying out for new buildings. Some of the temporary or portable buildings being used for educational purposes have seen their day, though they are still being used by nearly every school board in Canada. Something should be done in this regard. In addition to that new hotels are being built, and apartment houses erected, some of them no doubt under the priority system, and I am sure very heavy rents will be charged.
I have seen a good deal of this housing problem. I remember that after the first war we had the same trouble, as we seem to have it after every war-a huge shortage of all materials and labour. On the whole I believe a great deal of good work has been done in this world shortage of construction materials, and I am not here to blame or criticize anyone, but I should like to see this priority system discontinued particularly in regard to lumber, which has to do yvith one of our key industries. As the lumbering industry goes, so will go trade and commerce; so will go housing and many other matters. I hope the minister will use the regulations during the next three months in such a way that housing will be assisted, and the construction of hospitals, schools and similar public buildings may go on. These regulations were on the whole a good thing in wartime, not only for the industry itself but for labour as well; but now they should be dropped. To eliminate controls will help wholesale lumber dealers as well as the retail dealers, who have done very little business in the last few years. A great many of them I know do not make their office expenses. I remember in the district west of Bathurst street and north of Queen street when a great deal of house building was carried on; when Manning avenue, Euclid avenue, and all the other streets were built up as far as College, and all by private builders. They put up rows of houses all over the city, and I must commend the government on what they did to assist construction of this kind a few years ago. In 1935 we had a committee on reconstruction and housing whose report was later adopted in another form by the present government. At that time I advocated that money for house building should be lent through the banks at a very low rate of interest, about 3 per cent. Later the government spent about $90,000,000 in small housing,

Emergency Powers
a very large part of it in and near the city of Toronto. Many houses were built in East York, North York, West York, and the city district north of St. Clair avenue. In all that expenditure I believe the government lost only about $16,000. If they could embark on a scheme like that and lend money to private individuals and private contractors and give them labour and materials, I think it would be far better than setting up these costly crown corporations, which have to be administered from Ottawa, which get priorities on many materials and labour which small private builders cannot get, and then charge large sums in rental.

I have been sitting in the chamber now for quite some time, listening to this debate in general and to the discussion of this particular matter of housing. I have not taken part thus far because I live in a rural constituency where housing is not the same problem that it is in the larger urban centres. But throughout the discussion it has struck me that we may have missed some of the fundamental points in this whole matter. I refer now to the reason for the shortage of materials for housing. I have heard of the shortage of nails. I have heard of the shortage of lumber. I have heard of the shortage of this, that and the other thing. If such shortages were caused by physical forces over which we had no control, then I do not believe we could blame the minister. If these shortages had resulted from the war I would not attach a great deal of blame to the government. But it does seem to me that governments must take the responsibility of doing things for this country when it is physically possible to do them, and that seems to be the crux of this whole situation. Do I not speak the truth when I say that adequate housing has been held up because the government has permitted enormous amounts of housing materials to go out of the country? I do not think I am far wrong when I say that seems to be the reason.
I know there is a problem to be met. I have in mind, for instance, a family in which there were six boys, all of whom lived at home with their father and mother. When war broke out they enlisted. Before the war was over they got married and came back home, some of them with children. They wanted six homes of their own. I know that sort of thing creates quite a problem, and I am not saying the government is not faced with a problem. I am not one who would harshly criticize if a government were doing its best; but fundamentally is it not a matter of government policy? They have been so insistent on capturing foreign markets that they have permitted Canada to be divested of materials we ourselves need. If this parliament should conclude that such a policy is the right one, then let us not blame the government. If it is a wrong policy, then the government must should'er the blame for what is happening in the country today. That seems to me to be the reason. Since we are in committee I should like the minister to answer that question. Is there any physical reason why we Should not, with the war over as long as it has been, have a real housing programme on the way? If he says it cannot be done because of shortages, that is not enough. If there are shortages, let him tell the committee how they came about and what has prevented him from restoring these materials to free supply.
I am a great believer in the adage which we in this corner of the house so often quote, that that which is physically possible must be made financially possible. I am not going to talk about the financial possibilities but there should be no reason, apart from physical impossibilities, why the people of Canada cannot have what they want. Physical impossibilities arise only by reason of something over which we have no control. We have no control over winds, earthquakes, floods, and so forth; those are known as acts of God, things for which we would not blame the government. But if a thing is physically possible, why is it that the people of Canada cannot have it? That is the thing the government has to answer. I have not had an answer to that question, and I believe the government owes it to the people of Canada to give an answer. If we have that answered we will be satisfied.

Mr. Chairman, I can assure you that I shall be very brief. First I wish to associate myself with what
Emergency Powers

has been said by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, the hon. member for Royal and the hon. member for Halifax. The subject under discussion is one with which I am not particularly familiar, but I realize it is of great importance to New Brunswick and the other maritime provinces.
I have listened most attentively to this debate and must admit that the attitude taken by some hon. members is difficult to understand, particularly those who in one breath say that veterans' houses are costing too much, and bitterly condemn the government because they feel they are responsible for this condition; and then in the next breath they suggest that the retail ceiling price of lumber for domestic purposes is far too low and should be increased. The two statements do not dovetail. You cannot have your cake and eat it too. If we are to have higher retail prices for lumber, there will certainly be an increased cost to the veteran for his house.
My own personal opinion is that it is inconceivable that any producer should be obliged to sell his product at below the cost of production. Such a condition does not create a satisfactory atmosphere and no doubt in some cases would be responsible for black market trading. I am confident that this is not so in my own county, because no violations of this kind have been brought to my attention at any time.
I have a letter from a reliable citizen of Charlotte county which I believe will explain much better than I could the conditions in the maritime provinces with respect to the wholesale and retail lumber trade. The company with which this gentleman is associated, and which bears his name, has been doing business with the general public in Charlotte county and across the border in Maine for a great many years. I might add that this gentleman is a classmate of the Minister of Justice. This letter from the Haley Lumber Company Limited of St. Stephen, New Brunswick, is dated January 28, 1947, and reads:
I want to write you about the predicament we and the other retail lumber dealers of the mari-times are in due to the timber controls. You have probably read in the press that one of the woodworking factories had to lay off ten men because they couldn't get lumber.
The price paid by lumber brokers purchasing lumber to be exported to Great Britain has always controlled the domestic wholesale price in the maritimes. The present export price averages at least $52 per M. feet. One broker is offering a producer from whom we used to buy lumber $56 per M. for 2x4 and 2x6, $57 for 2x7 and 2x8, and $64.50 for 2x9 and up f.o.b.

St. Stephen in the rough. The present wholesale ceiling price averages $45 per M. feet, so you can see the impossibility of the retailers buying lumber at the wholesale ceiling price which is all they are permitted to pay.
A complicated system of earning export quotas was set up over a year ago for the purpose of encouraging lumber brokers or manufacturers-to sell to -the retailers and, in so doing, earn export quotas. The exporters and manufacturers haven't found it to their advantage to do this to any great extent. Sufficient free quota has been available to take care of the stock to be exported.
Over 90 per cent of the retailers in the maritimes have less than 40 per cent of the amount of soft wood lumber on hand to meet the demand for house building requirements. Emery Smith of Murray and Gregory told me he had only 500 M. feet of softwood lumber on hand and most of this was refuse. He should have-between two and three million.
The spread between the present domestic ceiling and the retail ceiling does not permit the retailer to purchase lumber at the market price, namely, $52 per M. feet, and sell within the retail ceiling and make a profit. The price paid for lumber to be exported has increased -at least $5 per M. in the last year without any corresponding increase in the domestic wholesale ceiling and the retail ceiling.
There seem to be three alternatives if the retail lumber dealers are to stay in business, satisfy their customers' requirements and carry on business without breaking any laws.
(1)	Decontrol of the lumber industry and' retain export control.
(2)	Increase retail ceiling prices by at least $5 per M. and cut out the wholesale ceiling; or
(3)	Increase the wholesale ceiling and allow" sufficient margin between the wholesale ceiling and the retail ceiling to permit the retailer to-make a profit.
Now, I hope you will do what you can to help out the retail lumber dealers who are in this terrible predicament due to price control.
Yours sincerely,
Harold B. Haley.
