speechtext:
The order in council
reads as follows:

At the Government House at Ottawa Tuesday, the 21st day of March, 1944.
Present:
His Excellency The Governor General in Council:
Whereas the Minister of Munitions and Supply represents that regulations respecting wood fuel were established by order in council P.C. 4362 of May 28, 1943, and were amended by order in council P.C. 5492 of July 9, 1943, and by order in council P.C. 215 of January 13, 1944; and by the said order
in council P.C. 4362, James S. Whalley was appointed wood fuel controller, and by order in council P.C. 1792 of March 5, 1943, Gustave
C.	Piche was appointed a deputy wood fuel controller;
That regulations respecting timber were established by order in council P.C. 2716 of June 24, 1940, and were amended by orders in council P.C. 7120 of December 4, 1940; P.C. 4389 of June 17, 1941; P.C. 6037 of August 8, 1941; and P.C. 7360 of September 20, 1941; and .by order in council P.C. 9994 of November 3, 1942, Alan H. Williamson was appointed timber controller; and
That it is desirable to abolish the office of wood fuel controller and to confer on the timber controller the powers, duties and functions with respect to wood fuel now being exercised by the wood fuel controller, and for these purposes to revoke certain of the orders in council above mentioned and re-enact regulations respecting timber as hereinafter set out;
Therefore His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, is pleased to revoke and doth hereby revoke the following orders in council:-
P.C. 4362 of May 28, 1943; P.C. 1792 of March 5, 1943; P.C. 5492 of July 9, 1943; and P.C. 215 of January 13, 1944.
P.C. 2716 of June 24, 1940; P.C. 7120 of December 4. 1940; P.C. 4389 of June 17, 1941; P.C. 6037 of August 8, 1941, and P.C. 7360 of September 20. 1941.
His Excellency in Council, on the same recommendation, and pursuant to the powers conferred by the War Measures Act and the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, is pleased to make the following regulations respecting timber and they are hereby made and established:-
REGULATIONS RESPECTING TIMBER 1. Interpretation.
(1) For the purpose of these regulations, unless the context otherwise requires, (a) "Controller" or "Timber Controller" shall mean the person appointed timber controller by the governor in council; (b) "Deputy Timber Controller" shall mean any person appointed a deputy timber controller by the governor in council; (c) "dealing in" shall include the following activities or undertakings and shall also include the doing of any act in preparation for or in the course of any of them;
buying, selling, exhibiting for sale, taking or receiving orders for, leasing, hiring, lending. borrowing, exchanging, acquiring.
Emergency Powers

the exercise or purported exercise of any power or authority from time to time vested in the controller.
7.	Powers of a deputy controller
A deputy timber controller shall have and exercise any and all powers conferred on the timber controller, subject to any restriction thereof which the controller may from time to time impose and subject in all cases to review by the controller; provided that any order of a deputy timber controller shall be final and binding unless and until it has been varied or vacated by the controller.
8.	Wartime industries control board regulations preserved
Nothing in these regulations shall restrict or vary the provisions of the wartime industries control board regulations established by order in council P.C. 3 of January 4, 1944 and the timber controller shall have the powers and immunities and be subject to the limitations granted and imposed by the said wartime industries control board regulations, which shall be read and construed as one with these regulations.
A. D. P. Heeney,
Clerk of the Privy Council. I
I would ask the minister to clarify his release No. 102 of April 22, because as I read it, it refers only to British Columbia and the western provinces, although the press has stated that the price of lumber is up 15 to 20 per cent all across Canada. I understood the situation, but evidently the press did not, and it was unfortunate that in several papers, including small papers in my own riding, the report went out to the country that lumber had increased in price 15 to 20 per cent.
Again in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec stumpage costs have been increased.
I would also like the minister to explain why an export quota of 65 per cent has been allowed to British Columbia as against 33J per cent for central Canada and the maritimes. Is the minister still consulting, as he did six years ago, the Canadian Lumbermen's Association which takes in all the lumbermen in Canada, or is he taking the advice of only one or two of the largest lumber operators?
I was in a retail office yesterday morning which had received a circular stating that an announcement would be made on lumber prices on the return of Malcolm McNicol. Wholesale and retail merchants are holding up sales in consequence until the announcement is made. Why could not this announcement have been made at the same time as it was made for

British Columbia and western Canada? If the timber control is efficient, and they have been working on controls for six years now and talking and thinking about prices and regulations, especially during the last six weeks, I would like the minister or his parliamentary assistant to explain why an announcement could not have been made to cover the whole of Canada at the same time. Why the hesitation and this discrimination against Ontario and Quebec?
I stated in the house in 1946 that the price of hemlock was then too low and it is still too low because it cannot be produced at the present ceiling prices. There have been increases in the cost of living and in wages and in everything which pertains to the production of lumber. At the same time we have lumber being imported from the United States to Canada to take the place of hemlock for crating at $77 to $82 per thousand feet.
I have a letter here which states that the Ford Motor Company:
. . . found it impossible to obtain sufficient crating lumber in Canada for their requirements and have been forced to buy substantial quantities of southern yellow pine, initial shipments of which are now arriving. This to take the place of Canadian spruce and jack pine which they have used heretofore.
At page 1234 of Hansard of March 10, 1947, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply stated that to increase the price of lumber would increase the cost of a house S200 or $300. Somebody had said that it takes approximately 6,000 or 7,000 feet of lumber to build a house 28 x 28 or 28 x 30. If the price of lumber were increased $10 the cost of a house this size would be increased $60 or $70, which would be approximately one per cent of the price of a house such as government agencies are building today for sale to the veterans. But would it not be worth it if they could get the lumber when they needed it?
The delivery of lumber could be speeded up and a lot of bottlenecks done away with. At the present time when you sell lumber you must send four copies of a document to the timber control, and on their approval and return you can start to ship the lumber. If something could be done to speed up that process it would help considerably. I do not know just what suggestion to make, but something should be done to speed up shipments.
I want to say a word on the export of lumber to Great Britain. The exports have been at exorbitant prices, ranging from $80 to $275 per thousand f.o.b. mill, with $3.25

Emergency Powers
added per thousand for rail shipments. We have been lending money to Britain without interest and selling our farm products to Britain at far below the world market prices, at the expense of the Canadian farmer. The government have told us that this will hold the British market for years to come. Is the case any different with lumber going to the British market? It does not seem to me good business to sell our farm products at a low price to Britain and then charge exorbitant prices for lumber shipped to Britain if we want her trade in the future. If the export prices on lumber going to Britain were reduced it would help to balance the low farm prices received on British contracts. At the present time we have to have an export market for our lumber. You could raise the domestic price on certain grades of lumber, especially hemlock, so that we could sell our lumber to Britain more cheaply and cinch that market. Russia, Sweden, Norway and Finland are going to compete against us in that market unless there is good mutual feeling between the lumber dealers of Britain and Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have been
amazed this afternoon, as I was last evening, at the large number of pleas made by members on both sides of the house that the government increase today's retail prices of lumber. Many of us are not familiar with all the ramifications of the timber industry, but we are conversant with the fact that retail lumber prices have gone up sixty to seventy-five per cent at least, and perhaps more. That the hon. member for Halifax should be pleading for increased lumber exports, as he did a few moments ago, at a time when we cannot find the materials for house building is a fantastic situation. We are not beginning to get to grips with the problem at all. The only reason the hon. member is asking for increases in the export quota for his own area is that the producers of timber in that part of the country may capitalize on this squeeze which is going on in the foreign markets. There is no justification for allowing the export prices to continue, for the reason mentioned in part by the hon. member who just resumed his seat. We are actually killing the goose that lays the golden egg by extracting every nickel that we can from the foreign market now, but when the emergency is over we shall be going cap in hand asking these people if they would be good enough to buy our product.
I mentioned the British market.

Yes. That applies, of course, to all our customers, but I am glad to be corrected with respect to the British market. That is what the hon. member said.
The argument of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, the hon. member for Charlotte, and as I recall it, the hon. member for Royal, was that we again increase the lumber price ceiling here in Canada. The hon. member for Royal yesterday made the statement that the retail lumber firms were losing approximately $8 a thousand on their lumber sales. If that is so it is not because of the price at which they are selling the product, but because retailers are not getting sufficient wares from the wholesalers unless they are part of the wholesale connection. As I understand it, the trend in modern lumber retailing is for the timber operator to control the distribution from the cutting to the final selling of the lumber. There is some evidence of that in my own city, where certain yards apparently have larger supplies of lumber than others. It may be due to their wholesale and saw mill connections.
Under this order in council the minister has sufficient power to analyse the costs of all of the steps of the marketing of the finished product. To hear figures like S80 to $200 odd a thousand quoted for export lumber, or $70 a thousand on own retail market when I can recall that just before the war the retail market was able to sell lumber at S40 a thousand, shows that there is something incongruous in these figures.
The other evening I asked the minister to give me specific retail prices for five different lumber items based on the prices in 1939, 1944 and 1947. I have not forgotten that request, if the minister has, and I am again asking him to put these figures on the record. Today I am asking that he do something more. We have been conveniently vague in the committee on the question of various spreads in the prices from log to wholesaler, to retailer, to the ultimate market. I should like to have the minister give the representative prices today-I do not care what kind of timber he takes-so that we can get the relative spread of a log delivered at the mill compared with that log in the form of sawn lumber at saw miff prices. Then I should like the wholesale price to the retailer and the retail price to the consumer of the same article on a basis of price per thousand feet. These are figures which any laymen can understand.
In discussing the duties of the timber controller it is not enough to outline his extensive powers, unless he does something about them.
Emergency Powers

The other evening I put on the record-and it has been done by other hon. members-the increased net profits of one corporation, the Canadian Western Lumber Company, on the west coast, which had tripled its dollar profits between 1945 and 1946, and yet its whole record from 1939 down to the end of 1945, as contained in the manual of investments that I have before me, is one of diminishing production. The capacity of the Canadian Western Lumber Company saw mills on the west coast is 209 million feet per annum. In only one year in the last eight years did it hit that figure. That was in 1939, when it produced a little over 200 million feet. In successive years from 1939 to 1945, the last figures which are given in this book, production dropped until in 1945 it was only 60 per cent of what it was in 1939, and yet the balance sheet is exceedingly-
Why did production drop?

That is one of the enigmas the meaning of which perhaps the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply may be able to give. Certainly there is nothing wrong with the timber limits which this company possesses. Everything that it owns is exceedingly accessible. This volume says that its limits are all accessible to salt water. The description of its property may be found at page 1816 of the Moody manual of investments. It is not a matter of getting the logs to the mill. It is simply a matter of this corporation-I am singling it out because its figures are so significant-
Does the hon. member know where its limits are?

Yes. It is all in this record of Moody's at page 1816. I do not wish to read it to the hon. member; he may read it himself if he likes. The point I am trying to make is that while the annual production has continued to decline from 100 per cent capacity to 60 per cent of capacity, the net profits have been increasing. In large measure this is due in my opinion to the fact that the company is scalping on the market as it now exists, and that the timber controller has not examined adequately the profit sheet of this and other corporations which are in the lumber business.
I should like the minister to put on the record now, or as soon as convenient, the figures which I asked for the other evening. This afternoon I will ask for the relative prices of five staple commodities used in house building as between 1939 and 1947. The other figure I asked for was the price of any type of log in terms of thousands of feet, and carry

the price of the article through the various distributing channels until it finally gets to the consumer. I think we shall find the answer to the problem of high cost of housing in there somewhere.
All I can say to my hon. friend is that I shall be glad to look up these prices and give them at the next sitting.

I think the committee
is entitled to a full explanation from the minister as to why he feels it desirable to continue this timber control, and, since so apparently he does think it desirable, what he is going to do to make the timber control a bearable thing for the timber industry from coast to coast. I know it is a very difficult problem for him. All his timber controllers in the past year have found it necessary to resign; their tenure of office is becoming shorter and shorter, and I feel I must say to him that he must do better than this in the operation of the timber control if he is to justify its retention at all. We saw in the house last night, and again this afternoon, members getting up from every part of Canada, and in every case the complaint is the one I hear so much from people in the lumber business in British Columbia. In the opinion of those people who are in the business it is not possible for any central organization . to control so varied a product as lumber and get the best production and have a smoothrunning industry.

May I make a correction
in the hon. member's statement? That is not the opinion of the members in the C.C.F. group in this house. We feel that the timber controller can do a good job, but we are mighty certain that thus far he has not made a good start in doing a good job. There is a big difference.

As a matter of fact I am not at all surprised at the hon. member's intervention, because it never really crossed my mind that they would support what the timber industry feels is in its best interest.
We will not support profits like the Canadian Western Lumber Company's; it is scalping the market.
Restrict production and force prices up.

I can say a word about that. I am not saying now that the timber control should be taken off. I have not the information that the minister has available; I have available to me only the results of his policy. It might appear to me, as it

Emergency Powers
appears to many people, that we would be better off if the control were removed, but that is a responsibility of the government. I am not here telling them what to do-
What are you telling them?

-but I am here to tell the minister what is going wrong and what ought to be fixed. That is what I conceive to be my task this afternoon. What the matter is, as the minister knows, is not really the question of profit at all, certainly not so far as the mills in British Columbia are concerned. They are all making a profit, and everyone knows where it comes from. It comes from the export trade, where the price is necessarily kept very high in order to subsidize a domestic ceiling which is actually below cost of production of lumber in Canada. That is perfectly clear, and it is admitted, I think, by the minister. That is why I was surprised when the member for Regina City raised this question of the profits of a certain company, which, he suggested, was scalping on the market,-whatever that is,-and that annual production had declined although its profits had gone up. The hon. member need not worry about profits made by that company. I hope he was not trying to leave the impression with hon. members that these profits were made out of the Canadian people, that the domestic market was being scalped. The Canadian people are getting British Columbia lumber at about a $10 subsidy, the cost of production being about $10 per thousand above the domestic price. If the annual production of lumber from this company has dropped each year since 1939, we have had a war on. I imagine that in the first couple of years there was a shipping shortage and perhaps not so much was cut for the export market; and after that we had timber control. It is open to serious doubts, from some of the speeches made here, whether the control exeroised by the minister is maintaining production in the way that production could be maintained either without the control or perhaps with a different type of control or a different handling of control.
The truth of the matter is that the policy followed by the government in this timber control has demoralized the timber industry in, every province in Canada. I have in my hand press clippings of Vancouver papers, of April 23 and 24, and although we have not got further papers I presume there will be more items of this kind on the way. At the moment the minister's timber controller is out in British Columbia attempting to negotiate
some new kind of agreement with the people in the business there, apparently so as to increase the amount of lumber which is delivered to the domestic market and reduce the amount shipped for export.
The minister knows that it would not be necessary in the case of many a mill for the timber controller to go to Vancouver at all, if there were a change in the policy followed by the government. I can mention one example within my personal experience where an operator in Vancouver wanted to sell a larger percentage of his cut domestically in order that he might maintain his pre-war markets and sell to veterans and not disappoint other old friends in Vancouver. He found he was unable to do what he wanted and he was unable to do what good business practice dictated, because if he did, he would be losing money over all. He found he must sell export right up to the quota in' order to make a profit on his total annual sale.
That is one little example of the way in which this industry is being distorted. Here is a clipping from the April 24 issue of the Vancouver Province:
Various lumbermen here reported today their stand that they do not wish to deprive the Canadian market of lumber and would willingly sell more at home if a profit could be made.
Then in a report in the Vancouver Sun of April 24, the concluding words are:
Vancouver lumber spokesmen said the government and its officers should get out of the business of allocating and imposing priorities for lumber orders. They would like to see controls in the industry completely abolished, but they have little hope of this.
Are you in favour of that?
In favour of what?
Abolishing controls.

I have just gone to some trouble to explain that that would appear to me to be a very wise thing, but I am anxious to hear what the minister has to say on it. The minister is now before this house asking for the continuation of his timber control. I do not think the house should pass this item without some explanation by the minister as to the difficulties which arise under his control, and what he can do in the future to set them right and see that the industry is not demoralized, as it appears to be. Does that make my position perfectly clear to the hon. member for Eraser Valley?

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, to have interrupted without asking for permission. May I say to the hon. member
Emergency Powers

for Vancouver-Burrard that I agree with him that far, but I still do not know where he stand's on controls.
You will find out.

It appears also from this report that at one stage in these negotiations there was an arbitrary attempt to order certain mills in Vancouver to change the destination of their shipments without giving them any compensation for that order. This report says:
Mr. Uren today swung a haymaker at the lumber manufacturers with an order to several mills to cease loading shipments to overseas ports, reprocess, and turn the lumber over to him for Canadian use.
Mills receiving this order indicated they may defy the federal officer's dictum. It places them in conflict with signed and sealed contractual obligations, they counter.
In the report of the following day, April 24, it appears that more progress has been made and that the plan is something like this. First, the controller proposes that the domestic allocations should be increased from 35 to 40 per cent and probably to 45 per cent; second, that by way of compensation for that increase in the domestic quota, price increases be granted; the suggested amount is a ten to fifteen per cent increase, and in another newspaper report I have seen it suggested that the price might be advanced $7 to $13; third, that a system of "approvals" be set up. This apparently is a new system of priorities-
. . . to assure definite quantities to veterans' housing, railways, mines, shipyards and municipal, provincial and federal projects. Under this scheme mills would take orders from such "prioritj'" accounts, and then get them approved by timber control here. Each mill would have to supply a certain portion of its total cut to these "approval" buyers.
It appears from that report that we are to have three things:	first, an increase in the
domestic quota, which is something I should be very glad to see; second, an increase in the price, and apparently a fairly substantial increase, according to the newspaper reports; and third, a completely new system of priorities, called approvals, which I think the minister should explain to the committee if there is any truth in the report; because it seems that of the forty to forty-five per cent now to be retained in Canada, half is to be directed, under this approval scheme, to projects which the government approves; and the sawmill is to be able to supply only twenty per cent of its cut to its normal customers in its usual business way. At first sight it would appear

to me that that is going to complicate and demoralize the industry even further than has the practice up to the present time.
Just before I sit down I wish to place on the record some of the things which have been done to this industry as a result of this control, particularly as they relate to British Columbia. In the first place, before the war and before the era of controls we had in British Columbia two major markets. One was the United Kingdom market and the other was the domestic market. Under the stimulus of low freight rates through the Panama canal during the depression, and under the further and most important stimulus of the Ottawa agreements and the imperial preference, British Columbia built up for her lumber a large market in the United Kingdom. At the same time the whole industry geared itself to those two markets. A certain number of the mills are export mills. They are on tidewater and have facilities for loading into deep-sea ships. As I understand it, they used to sell, say, ninety per cent of their cut export and ten per cent domestic. On the other hand there was the other set of mills-the small mills this time, and many more in number-which all over the province had rail outlets for their lumber. They naturally served the domestic market and shipped' export only to convenience buyers or to get rid of some surplus that they had not been able to sell domestically. Naturally, their proportion of sales was just about in reverse, ninety per cent domestic and ten per cent export, or something of that kind. Also, we had on the Pacific coast, in addition to the best timber in the world, a system of grading and checking of our lumber which is unparalleled anywhere. In the Pacific lumber inspection bureau we had a body of inspectors whose certificates were accepted right around the world as proof that the lumber shipped was up to specification.
I might also say to the committee that you cannot control and set prices on lumber in the same way that you can control and set prices on wheat, because lumber is not a single commodity. There is all the difference in the world between the various grades.
Grain is produced by the small fellows and lumber is produced by the big shots.
Oh, oh.
That is not the distinction, of course.

That is the C.C.F. mentality.

Emergency Powers

The distinction, is simply this. I believe you have grade No. 1, grade No. 2 and grade No. 3 in wheat. But to compare a big timber, twelve by twelve, with a two by four, for instance, is like comparing a motor car with a railway engine. They are two different commodities.
I am trying to compare lumber with wheat; but go ahead.
You stick to wheat.

As I say, that is a difficulty in which the minister finds himself in trying to control this multifarious commodity. We have also heard from other hon. members-and I will not dwell on the fact-that if you subsidize your domestic market by *high external prices, particularly in the United Kingdom market, you are very likely to kill the goose that laid the golden egg.
The second last timber controller had this to say at about the time of his resignation. In a press report from Ottawa, dated August 9, Mr. David Rosenberry is quoted as saying:
"I disagree with the contention that we should make our export prices carry our Canadian losses," said the timber controller. "We cannot go on doing this and survive." "Domestic prices," he added, "were dollars below" the cost of production ... If Canadian lumbermen were forced to protect their interests by a steady rise in export prices, he maintained, then the day could come when Russia might go after the British lumber market and undersell Canada.
The government must bear that in mind in dealing with this question.
Now I go on, I hope briefly, to show the various ways in which the clear-cut business procedure of the lumbermen in British Columbia which I have outlined has been distorted and broken down by what hap-pended under control during the war. I have explained their domestic mills and their export mills. An export mill must sell forty per cent of its output in the domestic market, which it is not designed to do, and a domestic mill must sell sixty per oent of its product in the export market, which in turn it is not designed to do. That causes damage to the good will of the various operators, and damage to their future business. You have man after man in the timber business complaining that he is unable to fill orders, sometimes from old customers, and worried lest that may damage his good will in future. Then you have a most extraordinary development, in that all over British Columbia you find new little re-saw mills springing up, and people building dry kilns in conjunction with
them, which never would have occurred in normal times. This has happened because some of the established mills have closed down their kilns because they could not operate them without increasing their losses. At the same time you have a deterioration in the quality of lumber produced and in the grading. You get random lengths instead of the lengths desired by the customer. You get all sorts of technical compliance with the regulations but what really amounts to evasion. For instance, you have lumber sold as rough lumber, which is taken by the purchaser to one of these small mills where it is re-sawn, dried and sorted by the purchaser, with the additional cost added to the ceiling price. Then you have other cases of custom cutting, where the owner of the logs will make a special contract to cut those logs at a price which, because it is a special contract, is not within the regulations. Time after time one hears of lumber delivered in Vancouver, and perfectly within the law, at $60 or $70 a thousand where the ceiling price may be $30 or $40.
In all those ways timber control, while it has not cost the people on the Pacific coast any money, while they are not complaining that they do not get an adequate profit, has broken down their proper business methods, so they are complaining that their industry has been demoralized. These are the matters which, in my view, the minister should be turning his attention to now and correcting. If he feels that he must maintain the control let him at the same time make it possible for this industry to get along under business practices which will permit the operators to keep their self-respect and retain their future markets. It should be made possible for them to do the good job that they did before the war, and that they want to do in future. I hope the minister will tell us whether, in his view, it may be possible to get away from all these malpractices which I have outlined and which come under his control.

I should like to say a few words; I shall be very brief, because I want to hear the budget tonight. I have in my riding the largest logging camp in the British empire, as well as the largest cedar mill in the British empire.
So what?

The hon. member has all the profits from the pulp mills and so on in his riding. Let him take care of Comox-Alberni and I will take care of my constituency. I disagree with the argument of the
Emergency Powers

previous speaker, as I understood it. Apparently, according to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, certain mills only are to be allowed in the export market. That was his argument, as I understood- it.
No; that is not what I said at all.

It certainly took the hon. member half an hour to try and convince me of something else, then-. I should like the hon. member to tell me of one mill- and I am speaking now of any well-known mill-on the lower mainland which, prior to the war, did not sell on the market that paid best, whether it was domestic or export. He cannot name a solitary mill that did not do business in that way.
Of course, and that was my point; they cannot do that now.
And I understood the hon. member to be advocating that only a very few mills should be in that export market.
Oh, no.
All right; I hope to be able to say in ten minutes more than the hon. member said in thirty-five minutes, so leave me alone.
You are not as bright as usual.
Not as bright as he thinks he is.
Don't misquote me, and I will leave you alone.

Maybe I am not as bright as I think I am, but let me tell the hon. member -that more lumber is produced in my riding than in the whole province of New Brunswick, so maybe I know more about lumbering than he does.
You don't produce it; you just talk about it.
I have probably produced more lumber than you have.
Did you ever go out with an axe?

Probably if I got an axe I would be able to cut more than the hon. member for Royal, though I must admit I could' not cut our timber in British Columbia with an axe. We have timber in our country, not the little match-sticks you have in New Brunswick. The argument of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and the (Mr. Cruickshank.]
hon. member for Royal, if I understood it, seemed to me to be the argument advocated about a year ago by the hon. member for Vancouver North, that our domestic prices should be increased. The hon. gentlemen will correct me if I am wrong, but that is my impression. At that time we were in favour of the domestic price being increased, with the proviso that the lumber so sold should be made available to the people of Canada through the various retail outlets. So I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has missed the boat. We in British Columbia who represent lumber districts-and I hope the minister is taking this in

claim that in that province we are not getting distribution of our fair allotment of the lumber we produce. We believe -the ceiling price for lumber could be increased by a reasonable amount on domestic sales provided that, as I said a moment ago, it is distributed -through the various retail outlets.
It is customary in British Columbia-and I understand that this applies also to the prairie provinces-for lumber to be distributed through retail outlets rather than direct from the mills. What has happened is that the large mills are distributing direct, and the result is that local retailers throughout the province are unable to get any supply. Large lumbering operations are carried on in my riding, so it is not a case of just talking about it like some of the hon. members from New Brunswick. A farmer wanting to buy supplies for his farm may have to send his truck on a trip of one or two days to get 200 or 1,000 feet of lumber. If the retailers were getting their fair quotas of lumber the farmers or users of lumber could afford to pay an increase of from S8 to S10 per
1,000	feet rather than having to go long distances to get their supplies.
If I am not mistaken, this is the argument which was advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver North in his intelligent speech of a year ago. He knows something about lumbering because lumbering operations are carried on in his riding. Personally I am opposed to the export market being granted to three or four large producers of lumber. A financier from Ontario came out to my riding and paid millions of dollars for one mill. If I am not mistaken he paid $14,000,000 for another outlet, although I may be wrong in my figures. However it ran up into the millions. Why did he do this? He did it in order to get the vast majority of that export market. This is one of the parties who said that they could not pay an increase of fifteen cents an hour to the loggers. I shall have something more to say about that later on.

Emergency Powers
I just wanted to impress upon the minister that, in so far as the people of my riding are concerned, they are prepared to pay an increased price on the domestic market, provided that the quotas are raised to permit the retailers, who are the normal outlet for supplies, obtaining the necessary supplies.

I feel I must accept the challenge of the hon. member for Fraser Valley when he referred to the size of the mills and the logging operations in his riding and compared them with the size of the mills and logging operations elsewhere. I feel that he has put his finger on the crux of the whole problem, namely, the neglect to channel domestic lumber through the retail merchants. I know that on Vancouver island the lumber yards have been short of lumber, with the result that the farmers and agriculturists who wanted to erect barns or some other type of domestic building have been unable to secure the small amounts of lumber which are absolutely essential to them.

Mr. Chairman, what I have to say now will probably not fit in too well with the wonderful discussion with regard to lumber to which we have been listening. I do not live in a lumbering district and I have not the same interest in lumbering as some of those who have spoken. But I do know that in my district lumber is in more or less short supply; it is very hard to get and it is very much in demand.
I wanted to say a few words on firewood. I live in southern Ontario where we have not a great lumber region any more but where firewood and wood for fuel purposes generally is very much in demand.
Emergency Powers
If I might interrupt my hon. friend, the control of fuel wood was dropped at the urgent request of the opposition.

Many people are deeply concerned about the cost of firewood, which is in real and urgent demand by a great many of our older residents. They love the odour of wood smoke and believe no other heat is as radiant or cheering as that from the open wood grate or kitchen range. They also dread the danger of coal gas and its deadly fumes and cling to the use of wood fuel for both its cheering comforts and safety. During the war years we had a fuel controller who divided our country into regions or zones and regulated the movement and prices of wood fuel according to its several standards. But price control has been removed from wood fuel. The title of P.C. 1997 which we are now debating is:
Order in council abolishing the office of wood fuel controller, transferring his duties to the timber controller and reenacting the regulations respecting timber.
And paragraph (h) of the interpretation clause of the regulations respecting timber
issued under that order in council reads:
"Timber" shall include any trees, standing or cut and any lumber in any form, and any wood, processed or unprocesseu, and any wood product, and any by-product, of wood, including but without limiting the generality of the foregoing, pulp wood, pulp wood chips, cordwood, millwaste, sawdust, hogged fuel and charcoal.
From this I conclude that, although controls have been removed from fuel wood, the order in council grants to the timber controller power and authority again to enforce price ceilings and other controls of fuel wood if he deems it in the public interest. Since the Minister of Justice has stated that numerous articles which have been removed from price control are decontrolled only so far as prices remain reasonable and just, and since coal strikes in the future are pending and there is uncertainty as to future fuel supplies, would the minister inform us if P.C. 1997 would give the timber controller authority again to enforce price ceilings on wood fuel if it advanced to such prices as, in his opinion, would not be reasonable and just?
At present flood control and soil reconversion are being given close and immediate study in the many recent flood areas and since forests play a large part in the scheme of flood control, there is danger, if timber prices advance too sharply, of finding an undue destruction of our fast vanishing southern forests. This is a matter of immediate concern and one that requires both federal and provincial study.

I think the way in which we handle this great natural resource of timber is the acid test of our democracy. We have in this country a timber cut of around four billion feet. During the last few days the question of controls has been under debate and we are now discussing particularly the utilization of our timber cut. My Tory friends to the right with their usual arguments have, in my opinion, been sidestepping the main issue. Their arguments represent a mental tango.
What is the main issue?

The
issue is this. We want to build houses for our people. I heard the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard ask a question of the hon. member for Regina City in regard to the profits being made by lumber companies. He asked: Does the hon. member realize that the Canadian people are not paying for the profits of the large lumber companies in this country. Was not tbat my hon. friend's question?
Yes.

The
truth is that the people of this country are paying for those profits. In a previous debate in this house I mentioned the profits of the H. R. MacMillan Company, a large lumber operator on the coast, which made a profit of
SI,300,000	in 1946 over 1945, and at that time the hon. member for Kamloops asked me if I realized what taxes this company had paid. I am not concerned with the taxes these lumber companies have paid. They are making tremendous profits. I would remind the government that before the election they promised that the veterans coming back would not be any worse off than the people who had stayed at home, and they promised the veterans homes and jobs. This is the acid test of democracy. Here is one of our great natural resources which the members of this group believe must be so handled and planned as to enable homes to be built for our people. But what have we today? A new timber policy has been announced by the press. The press reports that the cost of lumber is going up twenty-five to thirty per cent. If this is true the veterans will have to pay through the nose to get the lumber they need for their houses, and when you remember the small gratuities they receive you will realize that they will not be able to build houses if lumber increases in price. I have travelled across this country and have seen veterans living in basements in Vancouver. I know people in Ottawa who are living under conditions which,
i

Emergency Powers
if investigated, would be reported' as not fit for habitation. My information is that on the Toronto waterfront O'Keefe's, a large brewing company, are building a plant costing $2,000,000, which will use timber and other building materials, and that another is planned for Waterloo, and others elsewhere across this country. I think, therefore, it is high time that there should be planning of this great natural resource of timber so that it can be madte available to the people of this country as the members of this group have consistently argued.

Perhaps I should answer a few questions that have been asked. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent asked if it would be possible to reinstate the control of wood fuel under the present order in council. I am advised that it would be possible. We would have to call the control by another name perhaps, but it would be possible to reinstate wood fuel control under the order. I sincerely hope that will not be necessary.
The work of the timber control has been criticized. It is not surprising that there should be criticism when we hear the diverse views that have been expressed by the committee. We have had speeches advocating a higher percentage of exports, speeches advocating more lumber for domestic use, speeches demanding lower prices for housing and a great number of speeches demanding higher domestic prices so that we would not ask the poor lumberman to sell below cost. However we have struggled on for a good many years in administering timber control. It may not have been convenient for everyone.
May I tell the committee an experience that surprised me? I went all the way to Edmonton about two weeks ago to attend a meeting of the representatives of all the lumber interests of interior British Columbia and the prairie provinces. We were wanting a larger proportion of the cut in that area and some changes in distribution which would help out areas that were not getting an adequate supply of lumber. I introduced the subject by making a speech setting out our objectives, and I said that if this could be obtained it would probably speed the end of lumber control. Someone said, "No one in this room wants lumber control removed," and no one challenged that statement. One of the men drove me home afterwards, and I said, "Is that the feeling of the gathering in the room, that they do not want lumber control removed''. He said, 'Certainly".
What reason did he give?

He believes it is for the good of the industry. I believe that is the real opinion of the industry so far as producers are concerned. I am quite free to admit that the retailers do not take that view; but I think the important part of the lumber industry, so far as the present situation is concerned, is the producers rather than the retailers.
That means control for how long; an indeterminate period?
I did not ask him that. I shall perhaps go back, call them together again and ask that question.
They were all Conservatives at that meeting?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Was that the speech in which you told Alberta to send down Tories if they could not send Liberals?

There is a reason for timber control which I have mentioned before. We need only compare domestic.prices and export prices to realize that it is having an effect on the Canadian economy. For example, common fir and hemlock, surfaced four sizes, is selling at the mill in Vancouver at $26 a thousand. It is selling at the mill for export at $70 a thousand; flooring, 1 x 4, is selling in Vancouver at $55 a thousand for domestic use and for export, at $150 to $170 a thousand; drop siding, 1 x 6, at $43.25 a thousand, for domestic use and $106 for export. I could give these spreads in greater detail to indicate the type of market we would be competing against without control. I could quote from the Cross weekly letter, dated Portland, Oregon, January 31, 1947, which says:
The market on finished uppers belittles description. Prices seem never to get so high that they never go higher, and a price unreasonably out of line today looks good tomorrow. Fir flooring has been sold this week at $190, mill, and drop siding and other items of corresponding size and grade have found buyers at $150, and in a few instances even more.
Why does not the timber controller take over the complete export market and handle both ends of it?

There is a reason for that. The export market has been in existence for a good many years. We had traditional markets and we believe that the trade should look after their traditional markets. The business has been conducted between the private buyer and the private seller.

It is a competitive business.

Emergency Powers

Yes. Throughout the war years and throughout the reconstruction years we have tried to interfere as little as we could with the competitive situation. We have tried as little as possible to interfere with the proportion of export markets that were maintained before the war. For example, in British Columbia the cut has always been distributed about two-thirds export and one-third domestic. The same proportion holds pretty well in the maritime provinces. Therefore we have been permitting about sixty per cent of the timber of British Columbia to go export; we have been permitting about sixty per cent of the timber cut in the maritime provinces to be exported.
How is the minister controlling exports now; under the export and import powers or under the timber control powers?

Under both. We have the export regulations and we also have the timber control regulations. One operates on instructions of the other. There is a timber control advice to import and export control of the earned quotas and permits are granted accordingly. The overriding control is the import and export control.
Under trade and commerce?

Yes. It has been represented to us certainly in the house and from a great portion of the eastern trade that an increase in domestic prices would improve the distribution and the supply situation. Personally I have my doubts, but in any event, so far as western Canada is concerned, we found it necessary to retain a greater proportion of the cut to serve Canadian markets. The demand for west coast lumber has increased greatly this year, due to large domestic car orders and due to demands of provinces, municipalities and other public bodies for effecting repairs to essential structures. Therefore we have negotiated with the central British Columbia and prairie operators to reduce the proportion of their exports, and we have allowed them to increase domestic prices which will give about the same return to the mill as they were able to obtain under the former system of distribution. We have been negotiating with the west coast mills to the same end. I am advised that agreement has been reached or will be reached shortly. The domestic quota of west coast lumber will be increased and there will be a corresponding adjustment in prices, and an adjust-

ment in the whole range of prices to effect a better supply of the top grades of lumber in the Canadian market.
Will there be an increase in the export quota of lumber from eastern Canada in proportion to what has been reduced in western Canada?

No, certainly not; we need more lumber in western Canada. The export of lumber from the maritime provinces is the highest of any part of Canada. I understood from the hon. member's speech that he did not know that, but that is the fact. So far as the maritime provinces are concerned the export is about sixty per cent of the cut.
We export one car for every two cars that we use in the domestic market.

That is so far as the earned quota is concerned, but there is a free quota to the United Kingdom, of which every cutter in the maritime provinces has a share, so that the net result is almost the opposite. Two cars are exported in the maritime provinces for one retained in this country.
Will an increase be given to the retail dealers?
The increase in the wholesale prices of the mill will, of course, be extended and will cause a readjustment of domestic prices. That is being worked out at the present time.
What I mean is, will a definite amount be detailed to the retailer? Will there be quotas on it?
All lumber is sold through retail licences.
They cannot get any.
We hope this extra quota held in Canada will provide a better supply.

Has there been any extension of licences issued to mills? I understand that a great many of the mills are allowed to sell retail which were not allowed so to sell before, and one result of the change has been to make it much more difficult for the retail dealer to get supplies.

I cannot say. The wartime prices and trade board has the issuing of retail permits, and I think the test is as to whether the applicant has retail facilities. If he has a yard that is capable of serving the retail cus-

Emergency Powers
tomers I presume he gets a retail licence, but that is a matter which the timber controller has not had under his supervision. I do not know whether I have answered all questions.

Last night in the minister's absence I asked a question with regard to birchwood in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. There are about a billion feet of it, I understand, and it is being affected by a disease called dieback. I understood that the minister of lands and mines of Nova Scotia had made representations to the department here, asking that the quota be increased to allow them to cut this lumber, which would otherwise be a total loss in a few years.

That is true. We were asked to set a free quota for infested birch. The difficulty is that the lumber from infested birch is exactly like the lumber from good birch, and the result would have been that all the hardwood cut in the maritime provinces would have been infested birch by the time it came on the market.
You do not know the people of the maritimes or you would not say that.

What I did suggest was that, after the quotas of last year had been filled, the timber controller would permit seventy-five per cent of the surplus cut to be exported, which seemed to us a very liberal proposal in that regard. It has not been accepted and I notice the cut in the maritime provinces is about the same this year as last year, so far as hardwood is concerned. But if an extra effort were made to cut more infested birch, at least 75 per cent of it could be exported.

I have sat here and listened to the discussion that has been going on, and I resent some of the typically cheap C.C.F. insinuations against prominent industrialists in British Columbia. I certainly do not think they need to have me come to their defence, but what annoys me is the suggestion that we hear from across the way. Anyone not on direct relief, they seem to think, is an enemy of the state.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Who are the biggest recipients of direct relief?

With regard to Mr. H. R. MacMillan, may I say to my good friends the hon. members for Skeena and Assiniboia, that his record in British Columbia will stand close examination and will bear comparison with any of the records of members opposite in the C.C.F. party. He is a large employer of labour in my own riding, 83166-1624
and-I may say this for the information of my hon. friends-he told me not long ago that he was definitely opposed to the removal of the domestic price controls on lumber. He said he felt that the present controls were protecting the small man in the country who was trying to obtain a home for himself, and I thought he was acting in the manner of a good Canadian citizen. I want to put that on the record to his credit. The sawmill in my riding which Mr. MacMillan operates cuts a quarter of a million feet a day, and that mill has never turned down anyone in the riding when he required lumber for the construction of a home. They have seen that lumber was available to all the residents of the constituency. I might also say-

Will
the hon. member permit a question?

I might
also say to my hon. friend, when he is examining the facts with regard to lumber production and insinuating that some of the large lumber operators are reducing production in order to create larger profits because of scarcity, that the lumber cut last year in British Columbia was the largest in history, . and that we anticipate that it will be larger in 1947.

How much was
exported?

When
you refer to profits of that lumber company you would not be fair enough to inform the committee that there has been a vast expansion in that organization in the past year, involving millions of dollars of capitalization. There has been a large profit on the shipping business which that company carries on, something which has nothing to do with the domestic market at all. The lumber companies in British Columbia are considered the best employers of labour there. They have the highest scale of wages of any industry in the whole dominion.
I would say to the minister, however, that the British Columbia timber industry is highly competitive on the world market and our competitors have always been the United States mills on the Pacific coast. Because there is no price ceiling in the United States, and consequently they receive a high price for all their lumber, within the last three months there has been definite evidence that the Americans have been stealing some of our traditional markets from us, owing to the fact that they are able to undersell us on the world market. That is one feature of price control which must be considered in any
Emergency Powers

adjustment of the situation, but I am sure the minister will give these matters his close attention.

May I deal briefly with one statement made by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi, and that is the one about cheap C.C.F. insinuations with respect to the lumber barons, with whom my hon. friend is associated. There is nothing cheap about insinuations when they are supported with the figures of the tremendous profits that these people are hauling in.
They are taxed.

Assuming that they are
taxed; why should they not be taxed? You get your taxes where there is money. And whose lumber was it in the first place? Did the Canadian Western Lumber Company grow that timber? Certainly not; it is part of the domain of the people of Canada. Let me give instances of net profits, after taxes, in the case of the Canadian Western Lumber Company-and the source, by the way, is the Financial Post; there is nothing cheap about that. The Financial Post of March 8, 1947, quotes the Canadian Western Lumber Company as having received net profits, after taxes, in 1945 of $459,000 odd and in 1946 net profits, after taxes, of $1,019,000, or an increase of 121 per cent of actual profits. Let me say one thing more to my hon. friend. As to the rate of profit in 1946 on its capital of $3,073,000, how much of that is watered stock I do not know, but that is the capital-

The
original shareholders lost all their money, may I say for the hon. member's information.

The rate of profit was
thirty-four per cent. Well, that is not a very cheap insinuation. That is extremely high-priced stuff I am talking about. I know the effect on the producer, and you as a member of parliament and as a citizen of the country should know that our people are still suffering from lack of homes. That is the criterion by which we should be considering this matter in this house, and not only whether some lumber baron is paying proper wages to labour. I did not interject that.

The
hon. member for Comox-Alberni saw fit to get up and attack some of the statements I made, and I saw some of my hon. friends across the way and some to the right get up and support these tremendous profits. I do not think we have indulged in cheap propaganda

or debate or anything of that kind in this house. I have never in this house at any time reduced my arguments to personalities and I did not attack H. R. MacMillan for any personal reasons at all. I say this: When we have such a crying need in this country for homes and for building materials, for any government or any hon. member to stand up and support profits which I have already indicated-because my hon. friends are always talking about taxes-is something I cannot understand. Again I state that H. R. MacMillan and Company last year, in 1944, made a net profit of 81,213,790. There is the proposition. Hon. members can get up and support that sort of thing if they so desire.

I just wish to say a word or two, because I represent a district that produces annually some 125 million or 130 million feet of lumber. Fortunately, we have not any of these wicked people in my riding. The lumber industry in my district is largely owned by hardworking people, small people. I represent a riding which has many small mills in it. I have lived for some forty odd years with these people and I must say that they are splendid people to represent. There are some reasons for increasing costs as far as our district is concerned. I have found 'that our operators were on the whole very considerate of the local market and pleased with the profits they could make in the export market. These reasons are apparent when you consider the fact that just when the war opened-and I am giving this as an illustration-the stumpage on white pine on most government lumber was SI per thousand and at the present time it runs from $5 to $7.50 to 88 a thousand; the royalty has increased from fifty cents a thousand to $2.50 to $3 a thousand; operating costs have increased generally; wages have been considerably increased during the last three or four years.
I have some knowledge of the lumber industry and the problems of the operators; and they are all small operators. We have not a single large mill in my constituency. They are nearly all workingmen, working together in small operations or in individual operations. On the whole, I think it is quite safe to say that there has been no profit in the domestic market. They have been supplying the local market, and I think in most cases, with very few exceptions, they have been very fair about it. But they have obtained most all their profit in the export market. I am not sure what lumber prices are, but I can illustrate the point by giving one instance. Late

Emergency Powers
last fall we supplied cedar fence posts to the prairie market for which we were receiving fifteen cents apiece. The Americans were coming from the south of the line and offering us thirty-six to forty cents for that identical fence post. That shows where the profit lies. Consequently, everyone is human and tries to sell as many as possible to the export market.
I am pleased to know that the government is going to divert a greater proportion of the lumber to the domestic market where it is required. I do want to emphasize the fact that, so far as the domestic market is Concerned, I think the majority of the operators I represent have been very reasonable and fair and in some cases, have put themselves out in order to try to assist people who wanted to build. Ours is a decentralized type of lumber industry, because it is not possible to operate in a large way on mountain slopes and in mountain valleys. I think the results are a good argument for decentralization. The workingman there is involved in the operation of the lumber industry.
Before I sit down, I should like to ask the minister two questions. If a mill is selling retail from the mill direct rather than through a retail yard-we do not have such things; there are very few retail yards in the interior -is that mill allowed to sell at the price established for sale from the retail yard or not? And what is the price now established for the interior industry, for three or four grades of lumber retail?

A mill can sell retail if it holds a licence to sell retail. In other words, if the wartime prices and trade board have decided that it is entitled to it, that it can give retail service, a licence is issued to the mill and it is allowed to charge retail prices. Otherwise it can sell only at mill prices. I did not catch the second question.
Can the minister give the retail prices now of three or four ordinary grades of lumber?

I just wish to ask the minister one more question. Would this price apply, for instance, in my own district if lumber was being sold by the mill retail to local customers?
No. This is the mill price, plus the freight, plus the mark-up for the retailer.
To the prairie provinces.

To the prairie provinces, yes. This would apply perhaps in Calgary, or between Calgary and Medicine Hat. Prices farther east are higher; for the central portion they are about $2 a thousand higher, and in the eastern portion about $2 a thousand higher again.

Will the minister explain this new system of approvals whereby apparently fifty per cent of the domestic quota is now allocated by the government? What is proposed by the government to be the quota?
Mr. * HOWE: The allocations system has been in effect since controls were established. During the war practically all domestic lumber was allocated to war uses. After the war ended, we attempted to get away altogether from allocations, but we never were completely successful. There were essential uses for which allocations were maintained, such as federal government uses and certain provincial government allocations. It has been found necessary recently to enlarge the sytem of allocations. I cannot believe that it will be fifty per cent of the domestic quota in any section of the country. For instance, we have a domestic car-building programme which requires special grades of timber. They are difficult for the mills to fill, and in order to get the lumber it has been necessary to allocate certain parts of the order to various mills. That is true of certain provincial requirements. The allocations system is fair in that; if it is an awkward bill of lumber to fill, each mill is required1 to take a portion of it. In other words, certain mills cannot take all the good and other mills take all the bad.

I just wish to say a word or two about this knotty problem of lumber. I do not know whether or not I can throw any light on the shortages that appear; but a week ago Saturday in London, in western Ontario, the Liberal association held their meeting. It was evident there also that a shortage existed of good lumber for political platforms. Some of it was shaky; some of it was knotty. So I would say that not only the
Emergency Powers

lumber dealers and the farmers require lumber; political parties seem to be having trouble finding good material for their platforms.
Would the minister agree that with the high export quotas on the east and west coasts the operators in central Canada are in a tough spot?

No. The operators in the central provinces are close to their markets; their prices are higher than on either coast, and in my opinion, for the size of their opera^ tion, they are just as 'well off as are operators on the west or east coasts. People assume that the well being of an operator depends entirely on the proportion of his exports. It depends, of course, on the combination of the price at which he sells in the domestic market and the price at which he sells in the export market; and I have not heard anyone suggest that the operators in the central provinces are not doing as well as any other timber operators.

Has any consideration been given to increasing the quota to retailers, in view of the new prices?
Mr, HOWE: Oh, yes. All lumber sold domestically is sold by retail, and if we increase the domestic quota we increase the supplies to the retailers.

I am sorry; I do not think the minister got exactly what I mean. In British Columbia we have a large number of retail dealers; I am not speaking of the mills with retail licences. Has consideration been given, to increasing the quotas to the retail dealers?
I assume that will follow automatically when large quantities are put on the domestic market.

The minister promised that before this item went through he would give me a reply to questions I asked with respect to typical prices. He gave that information in part when he gave the prices for certain sizes of boards in the prairie region, but to make the record complete I asked that he give prices for 1939, 1944 and 1947 for five types of material to which I referred on Friday, and this afternoon I asked that he add the prices of logs delivered to the mill. I do not care what type of logs they may be-fir logs, if you like, so that we may follow the one transaction through. Take a fir log at the mill, after it is milled, the wholesale price and the retail price per thousand feet.

The answer to that question will require a good deal of research. No one could have the prices at hand, in a complicated schedule like the lumber schedule, and be able to give an answer to that question in a few minutes. I shall be very glad to have the answers worked out and table them later. My hon. friend would not suggest that we hold up this item until he gets that information, but I will table it as soon as I can.
I asked for it on Friday, and I still have not obtained it.
I am told they are still working on it.

I would like to say a word before this item carries, though I do not intend to hold up the committee. There has been a great deal of discussion in regard to the prices of retail lumber. I am not in a position to say whether the milling companies are making exorbitant profits; I think the minister and the control officials should have that matter well in hand. But if it is true, as has been stated, that all the profits of these mills are being made in the export trade, then I have wondered just what would be the position of the man operating a small mill, and I think perhaps some investigation should be made in that regard.
The small man gets his export quota the same as the big man.

But it would not benefit
him to the same extent; his turnover would not be so great. That was not the matter I particularly wanted to mention, however. I am concerned about the price increase on domestic lumber sold through retail channels. I cannot bring myself to believe that the retail yards have been suffering so very much. I agree with the minister when he says, as I interpret his words, that probably more attention should be given the wholesale or producing end of it than the retail end; generally speaking I believe that is true. In the last little while retail prices have been steadily climbing. Not only is that true, but the retail lumber companies have been making profits in another way which is detrimental to the consumer, the man who wants to build a house.

a fellow come to my house while I was home at Easter, who wanted this question brought up. I said, "Why don't you give me a statement to that effect? Put it in a letter to me, so that I will have it in black and white." Their position, however, which I can quite understand, is that if they did anything like that they would not be able to get lumber at all from the retail yards.
Is this the same man who lays his flooring for three cents a square foot?

back on that argument, but if the minister says a man can lay flooring at 3 cents a foot or less and make a decent day's wages, I say he cannot do it.
