I turn now to corporation income and excess profits taxes. Effective at the beginning of 1947, these have been reduced to a straight corporation income tax of thirty per cent on profits, plus a tax of fifteen per cent on excess corporation profits. As my predecessor stated last year, the excess profits tax has distinct weaknesses and limitations in normal times and is not, therefore, to be accepted as a permanent part of our tax structure. As he said, the government decided last year that it would be retained for this year, 1947, unless provision is made for its earlier repeal at this session of parliament.

We have given careful consideration to the question of whether or not this tax should be repealed before the end of the year, and have taken into account the views and arguments advanced from many sides. If business conditions had now returned to normal and we could rely upon the forces of competition and bargaining to keep profits at normal levels, we would be justified in repealing this tax with effect before the year end. If business needed larger profits to encourage and enable it to provide additional employment by greater expenditures, we should repeal the tax forthwith. Neither of these conditions exists at present. While competition is returning and supply is catching up on demand, profits before tax still are running at abnormally high levels, due to the after-effects of the war, including continuing demobilization and export credit

The Budget-Mr. Abbott
expenditures. Business confidence and available funds are so high that a good many business men are competing more in their efforts to expand their investment quickly than in getting down their costs and keeping down the prices at which they sell their products. In all these circumstances, the government has decided that this tax should not be terminated until the end of the year.
A short time ago in this house I urged Canadian business men to reduce their prices as their volume and efficiency of business expand. I stated that it is neither proper nor even good business to charge all the traffic will bear. I want to emphasize that view again now. We in the government, and - the vast majority in this house and in this country, believe in what is now called "free enterprise". We believe in it not as a windy doctrine or a mystic ideology, but as a sensible way of getting things done. It must prove itself and justify itself by its results. With the orderly removal of controls, with increasing supplies of material, with efficient and cooperative labour, and with ample markets, Canadian business enterprise is in a most favourable situation. We all expect it to show its mettle, both in production and in marketing. We expect it to show its ability to keep down costs and prices. In its own long-run interest, as well as in the national interest, business must keep its prices down and its profits within reason.
While most of the minor amendments in our tax laws will be dealt with in the revised act, about which I have already spoken, there are a few changes applying particularly to corporations and other businesses which I wish to propose at the present time.
In the first place, I am proposing that we levy a 5 per cent withholding tax on dividends paid by wholly-owned Canadian subsidiaries to their parent companies abroad. We have no tax of this kind on such companies at present, but such a tax is permitted by our tax convention with the United States which levies such a tax, and we feel that it is not unreasonable for Canada to have one as well. This new measure is to come into effect immediately, and I estimate that in a full year it will yield three or four million dollars.
It is also proposed to extend for 1948 the allowances that have been made in recent years for expenditures on exploration for oil, gas and other minerals. We believe that these allowances have been important in facilitating and encouraging mineral exploration and development, and that we should continue them at least for another year. We propose to change the form of these allowances from
the present form of a tax credit to the more normal form of a deduction from income. In the case of the special allowance provided for expenditures on deep test wells, we will make a further special provision to preserve the equivalent value of the tax credit now granted.
In accordance with the announcement made several months ago, I am also proposing to introduce a special provision in the income tax law to ensure that the income content of funding or refunding security issues received by taxpayers after January 1, 1947, will be taxed as income in the year in which the new issue is received. As I explained in the announcement, we feel that it is necessary to take this precaution to safeguard our revenue and to preserve equity.
Other proposed amendments relating to the income tax act will remove the residence requirements for dependent wives and children, now possible after the war conditions are ended, and lengthen the period within which refunds of over-deductions may be claimed; make provision for tax credits to Canadian companies in respect of corporation income tax paid to a foreign government on income of a foreign corporation in which the Canadian company owns more than 50 per cent of the voting stock; amend the part of the act dealing with the undistributed income of private companies in several minor respects; and also amend one or two provisions of the act which must be revised to carry out the terms of the agreements with the provinces. I shall give explanations and details of these minor amendments when we are dealing with the resolutions. There are some other detailed provisions in the amending bill itself which can best be explained and discussed when we have it before us.

In the field of taxes on commodities, the only major change which I am proposing is to give effect to my earlier announcement that the gasoline tax of 3 cents a gallon will be repealed as from April 1. It is estimated that this tax would have yielded us close to $40 million in the current fiscal year, and I must, therefore, take account of this loss in our estimate of total revenue. It is, of course, well known that our purpose in withdrawing from this field of taxation at this time is to leave the provincial governments, which have traditionally occupied the field, full scope to carry out whatever policy they think best within it. As a result, the reduction in our tax may not result in any reduction in taxes paid by the consumers of gasoline, but that, of
The Budget-Mr. Abbott

course, is a matter for each provincial government to decide in its own case. Pending action by parliament, I requested the Department of National Revenue to suspend collection of the tax from April 1.
We are also proposing to make certain minor amendments in the tax on passenger transportation, to conform with recent changes in the corresponding tax in the United States. It is desirable in this field to preserve as much similarity as possible between the taxes in the two countries, as that simplifies greatly the position of our common carriers. We are also proposing to iron out certain minor anomalies in the structure of the sugar tax and to make certain technical changes in the Act to improve its effectiveness.

I have already referred to the tariff negotiations now taking place in Geneva. These are of the greatest importance to Canada. We hope and expect that out of them will come sufficient reductions in tariffs to make it practicable to establish an international trade organization and to agree upon a code of international behaviour in regard to import restrictions, export subsidies and other commercial policies. Canada is, of course, prepared to make tariff reductions and reductions in preferences in exchange for tariff reductions by the United States and by other countries. We do not expect one-sided bargains. We are ready to do our full share.
I feel it is important, however, to stress two aspects of the situation from the Canadian viewpoint. In the first place, the tariff policy of the United States is the key to the success both of the tariff negotiations themselves and of the proposed charter. All of us who buy from the United States on a large scale and who owe large sums to the United States on capital account must have a greater opportunity to sell our goods in her markets than we have had up to now. Unless large scale American imports provide the world with an adequate supply of United States dollars, the rest of the world cannot hope to follow the liberal, multilateral and non-discriminatory trade policy which the United States has been urging upon it with our support and that of others. A positive lead in real tariff reductions by the United States is, therefore, needed if success is to be achieved at Geneva.
Secondly, there are in the proposed trade charter a good many qualifications and escape clauses applying particularly to the vitally important parts of the agreement that relate to quantitative restrictions on trade. Good arguments can be made, and are made, for

each of these. But we must guard against the danger that if too many of them are included in the charter, the sum and substance of them all, taken together, may undermine many of the positive benefits which the charter is intended to give to each of the agreeing countries.
These are two points that deserve our keenest attention in regard to the negotiations and charter discussions at Geneva.
In view of the negotiations now in progress, I do not propose to recommend any tariff changes in this budget, nor to make any detailed statement of tariff policy. I should, however, remind the house at this point that during the past year a number of special wartime tariff arrangements have ended with the end of the special wartime circumstances that gave rise to them.
Various orders in council which had provided for temporary reductions or suspensions of duties on individual items to make it possible to hold price, ceilings, were revoked from time to time as ceilings were removed, or as domestic supplies improved. This process was virtually completed on March 31. Moreover, as I announced last January, provision has been made for the issue of a proclamation on June 30, 1947, terminating the reductions of duty under the War Exchange Conservation Act. This will restore the regular British preferential rates of duty on imports from the United Kingdom. Our future trade relations with the United Kingdom, the United States and other countries will be determined in the light of the outcome of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Employment.

Before taking into account tax changes, I have forecast revenues of $2,450 million, and expenditures of $2,100 million for the current year, leaving a prospective surplus of $350 million. The reduction in taxes now proposed, including the repeal of the gasoline tax, will, it is estimated, reduce our revenues by a total amount of $265 million when they are in effect for a full year under economic conditions similar to those at present. Consequently these proposed tax changes will effect a continuing reduction in the general level of our revenues equal to approximately three-quarters of the amount of the surplus now in prospect. This, I believe, is as great a reduction in our tax structure as we should make at the present time. It is too early yet to hazard any forecast as to the probable level of expenditure and revenue in the fiscal year commencing April 1, 1948, but I believe

The Budget-Mr. Abbott
it would be most unwise to carry our tax reductions at the present time beyond those which I now propose.
The effect of the proposed tax reductions upon revenues in the current year is estimated to be approximately S160 million, reducing them, therefore, to a total of $2,290 million. After allowing for our prospective expenditures of $2,100 million, this leaves us with a prospective surplus of S190 million and a corresponding prospective reduction of that amount in our net debt during this fiscal year. I should point out that on the basis of the foregoing estimates, were the tax reductions in effect for the whole of the current year, this apparent surplus would be reduced to $85 million.
In appraising this prospective surplus, however, one must keep several factors in mind. In the first place we must be prepared to make financial provision for agreements with any of the three remaining provinces which have not yet signified their desire to do so but who may wish to enter into such agreements. Should all three provinces entertain agreements effective this year, our expenditures will be increased by an addition $110 million or thereabouts. If they do not, then we can reduce our net debt correspondingly. Secondly, it must be borne in mind that our revenues now are very sensitive to any change in general business conditions. In forecasting them in this budget, we have assumed that our national income, production and trade will be at high levels. We believe that this is the most probable course of events. On the other hand, it must be conceded that some recession in the United States this year is by no means impossible. A substantial recession in that country would be bound to have some effects on our own situation, and this in turn would adversely affect our revenues. We must, therefore, leave some margin of safety in the form of a surplus, which we will apply to debt reduction, if conditions remain favourable.
I hope that it will be a cause for gratification and confidence to members of this house and to all Canadians that we are able to drop the tax on gasoline, make a very substantial reduction in our personal income taxes, and still show a prospective surplus in our accounts. This is convincing evidence of the inherent strength of our financial position. I would be less than candid, however, and derelict in my duty, if I did not point out that this favourable situation is due in a very large part to the generally favourable
economic circumstances upon which our revenues so greatly depend. If and when we face greater economic difficulties we must anticipate lower revenues. We may also, I hope, anticipate somewhat lower expenditures within a year or two, as certain of the abnormal post-war expenditures disappear, particularly those on subsidies and veterans' benefits. On the other hand, the reduction in these expenditures may be offset in some years by other expenditures deliberately undertaken for the purpose of improving employment and incomes. Consequently our favourable positiQn this year cannot in itself be taken as evidence that we shall be able to avoid deficits in future years when economic conditions are less favourable than now.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to present a balanced view of the financial affairs of this country. I have explained the extent to which our current prosperity and our governmental accounts have been influenced by factors of a special, abnormal or temporary nature. I have dealt with several of the major problems which still confront us and which we must solve if we are to retain a healthy and prosperous economy. But in spite of all I have said to discourage undue optimism or complacency, the story I have had to tell is one, I repeat, which should justify pride and inspire confidence in every Canadian. We can take just pride in the size of the surplus I have reported, pride in the fact that it has been achieved so promptly after the end of the war, pride in the fact that after a 51 per cent cut in personal income taxes and other drastic reductions from the peak of wartime taxation, we are able to forecast better than a balanced budget for the new fiscal year. All this bears eloquent witness to the speed and smoothness with which we have made the transition from war to peace. It reflects the health and the underlying strength of Canada. It inspires faith and confidence in the future of a country which is responsible for such great achievements following the close of a war to which it devoted its resources without stint on a scale matched by few others.
Two months hence we shall have occasion to celebrate the eightieth anniversary of the founding of this confederation. It was seventy-nine years ago yesterday that the first formal budget speech was presented to this house by the then Minister of Finance, the Hon. John Rose (later Sir John Rose). On April 28, 1868, in a speech lasting nearly four hours, he presented his estimates of revenue and
The Budget-Mr. Abbott

expenditure for the first fiscal year of the new Dominion and outlined his financial proposals for the following year.
There was no Hansard in those days, but, according to the Ottawa Times of the following day, there were loud cheers when he expressed the view that "unless something very extraordinary or unforeseen should arise", the year would show a surplus on ordinary account, excluding capital expenditures, of $374,140, estimated receipts of about $14,700,000 exceeding estimated ordinary expenditures of $14,300,000. No doubt with a praiseworthy effort to improve the lot of succeeding finance ministers, he attempted to refute the charge that the country was "groaning under a heavy load of debt and taxation" but in any case it is interesting to note that eighty years ago it was also the custom to claim that the country was going to the dogs because of high taxes and high debt. The whole spirit of the speech can be summed up in a phrase which the minister had used on a previous occasion- "the sums we have to deal with are considerable but the resources and energy of the country are ample to meet them".
These men of 1867 had faith in the future of the united Canada which they were then striving to build. But probably none of them ever dreamed that in eighty short years, total revenues of the dominion could expand nearly two hundred times. We have indeed travelled a long way from the small beginnings of those days. But the same qualities which have brought us thus far can carry us to still greater heights. We are entering a most exciting period. Never before have there been such great material opportunties open to any generation. Never before have we been so conscious of the challenge presented to our economic and political abilities. Never before has our country been called to occupy a position of such high responsibility in world affairs as she does today. If we continue to show the courage, the unity and the spirit of cooperation which inspired the fathers of confederation, and which inspired our peope during these last war years, our achievements in the peace-time years ahead will, I am confident, be equally striking.

(a)	be removed in respect of transportation by vessel or aircraft extending outside of the northern part of the western hemisphere, except in respect of any part of such transportation that is between any port or station in Canada or the United States and any other port or station in Canada or the United States; and
(b)	be extended to apply in respect of all transportation by vessel wholly within the northern part of the western hemisphere;
and that the second proviso to subsection (l)ot section 32, under which section the tax is imposed, be repealed.
2.	That the tax on syrups enumerated in Customs Tariff Items 139 (except glucose and grape sugar) and 140 (except molasses) be reduced from 2 cents per pound to 1 cent per pound.
3.	That the provisions relating to the imposition of the consumption or sales tax on the sale price of goods be amended to provide that where the sale price is payable in instalments, the tax will be payable pro tanto at the time of payment of the instalments whether or not there has been physical delivery of the goods.
The Budget-Mr. Abbott

4.	That payment of sales and excise taxes be required without refund in respect of taxable goods purchased or imported for commercial or mercantile purposes by provincial governments or agents or servants thereof.
5.	That payment of excise tax be required in respect of any performance, exhibition or contest that includes professional performers, horse races or motion pictures when held, staged or
operated by the institutions, boards or other organizations mentioned in subsection (2) of section 122 of the said act.
6. That the excise tax on gasoline of three cents per imperial gallon be repealed effective on and after April 1, 1947.
7.	That the enactments founded on this resolution, other than paragraph six come into force on the 30th day of April, 1947.

3.	Although the accounts are not yet closed, it is estimated that grand total revenues for the fiscal year 1946-47 will reach $2,984,271,000. While this indicates a decline of $28,914,000 from the previous year's grand total, it should 
be borne in mind that the grand total for each year contains a large amount of special receipts and credits from bookkeeping transactions arising out of the war and the sale of surplus war assets. Such items, which have been abnormally high in the last three fiscal

The Budget-Mr. Abbott
years, are largely non-recurring. Because of such items a comparison of grand total revenues is not as significant as a comparison of ordinary revenues which in 1946-47 exceeded the total for the previous year by $249,028,000 and was indeed the highest in Canada's history.
4.	Throughout 1946-47 tax revenues have been remarkably buoyant and despite tax reductions the total revenue from taxes was higher than in the previous year. Total direct taxes on personal and corporate incomes yielded $1,405,600,000 or 47-1 per cent of total revenues. Excise taxes and duties also held a very important position contributing $775,000,000 or 26-0 per cent of the total. Customs import duties provided $237,400,000 or 8-0 per cent. Non-tax revenues aggregated $160,880,000, and there were special receipts and credits amounting to $372,071,000.
5.	The amount of $7,200,000 was set aside as a reserve for the refundable portion of excess profits taxes and this has been deducted in arriving at the revenue total given above. The distribution of these reserves is set out in the section relating to excess profits tax.

6.	The personal income tax which yielded $695,000,000 was again the largest single source of revenue. Despite the substantial reductions in tax rates which were in effect the receipts were slightly higher than in 1945-46, reflecting the very high level of employment and increased incomes during the year. A further influence was the considerable number of servicemen who began to receive taxable incomes as they returned to civilian employment.
7.	Corporation income tax and excess profits tax which are both levied on business profits yielded a combined total of $687,700,000 which was $24,330,000 less than the previous year's
combined total. The corporation income tax yield of $239,000,000 was $21,166,000 more than in the previous year while the excess profits tax yield of $448,700,000 showed a decline of $45,496,000. The lower return from the excess profits tax reflects the changes announced in the 1945 budget which became effective on January 1, 1946. An important factor causing the yield of the corporation income tax to increase was the receipt of substantial amounts in 1946-47 from private companies paying the tax on accumulated undistributed income as provided by Part XVIII of the Income War Tax Act.
8.	The liability of corporations to pay refundable excess profits tax was lifted after January 1, 1946, but those which had fiscal year ending after that date were required to pay, during 1946, this tax on a part of their profits proportionate to that portion of their fiscal year which fell in the calendar year 1945: The amount of refundable excess profits tax and personal income tax reserve classified by the taxation years to which it relates, is shown in the table below. The amount of reserve established in the fiscal year under review was $7,200,000 and this was entirely on account of the excess profits tax. 11.	Net revenue from customs import duties reached the unprecedentedly high total of $237,400,000 and exceeded the previous year's yield by $108,523,000. Industrial reconversion, high consumer purchasing power and insistent demand for goods long in short supply have tended to increase imports and this increased volume of imports, together with the higher money value upon which customs duties were levied have brought substantially increased revenue from this source.
12.	Excise duties which are levied exclusively on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products brought in a total revenue of $196,000,000, an increase of $9,274,000 over the previous year. Most of this increase was contributed by alcoholic beverages. The smoker's contribution to the Federal Treasury continued to be large with the over-all revenue from tobacco products (including the yield of the additional taxes imposed under the Special War Revenue Act on tobacco, cigarettes, cigarette papers and tubes, pipes and smokers' accessories) amounting to $184,161,000, which is 7-5 per cent of total revenue from taxes.
13.	The heading "Excise Taxes" includes the wide variety of commodity taxes levied under the Special War Revenue Act, of which the sales tax and the taxes on tobacco products were the largest sources of revenue in 1946-47. Gross collections were $2,037,000 lower than in the previous year, but because refunds of excise taxes have declined from $114,878,000 in 1945-46 to the more normal peacetime figure of $29,878,000 for >1946-47, the net revenue from excise taxes was $82,090,000 higher in 1946-47 than in the previous year. When it is considered that the war exchange tax which yielded $41,198,000 in 1945-46 was not in effect in 1946-47, this increase in total net revenue from excise taxes is all the more notable, reflecting greater supplies of goods, a somewhat higher price level and a continuing high volume of purchasing power in the hands of the public.
With a few minor exceptions, all excise taxes showed an increase in 1946-47. The tax on furs which was changed in October, 1945, from 25 per cent at point of dressing with no sales tax, to 10 per cent and sales tax, showed a decline. The war exchange tax and the tax on electric and gas appliances which were not in effect during the year yielded only insignificant clean-up amounts. The gross revenue from sales tax increased slightly, but

as a greater part of the refunds of excise taxes are in connection with the sales tax the net yield from this source showed a considerable increase. The net yield from the sales tax continues at a very high level despite the changes in 1945 which excluded equipment and apparatus used in production as well as building materials from this tax.

Bonds and debenture stocks bearing the guarantee of the Dominion and outstanding in the hands of the public, totalled $566,954,000 at March 31, 1947, an increase of $25,972,000 over the amount outstanding at the close of the previous fiscal year. This increase is occasioned mainly by -the issue and sale to the public of $50,000,000 Canadian National Railway Company 2£ per cent Bonds dated January 2, 1947 and maturing January 2, 1967 and the redemption of $23,752,000 Canadian Northern Railway Company 6| per cent Bonds on July 1, 1946. The new issue was sold to a syndicate of Canadian banks and bond dealers at a price of 99-68 per cent to the Company. Of the proceeds of the issue the sum of $41,932,257 was used to pay off loans from the Government and the remainder for capital purposes of the Railway.
60.	Pursuant to the terms of an Order in Council dated April 16, 1946, the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation was authorized to guarantee certain advances and interest thereon obtained by any person from a bank in order to purchase coal, coke or briquettes in the summer of 1946. The liability of the Corporation is limited to ten per cent of the aggregate advances made by each bank, but the maximum amount of guarantee is $500,000. The estimated contingent liability of the Corporation at March 31, 1947 was $26,000.
61.	Under the provisions of The Farm Improvement Loans Act, 1944, the Government guarantees loans made by chartered banks to farmers for authorized purposes. The
amount of the guarantee is limited to 10 per cent of the aggregate principal amount of the guaranteed farm loans made by each bank. At February 28, 1947, 18,945 loans had been made by the chartered banks in the amount of $14,496,864 and the contingent liability of the Government at that date was $1,449,686.
62.	Under the provisions of The Veterans' Business and Professional Loans Act proclaimed on January 15, 1947, the Government guarantees loans made by the chartered banks to veterans domiciled in Canada for authorized purposes. These - purposes include the purchase of a business, the purchase or repair of machinery, tools, instruments or other business equipment and the construction, repair or alteration of or the making of additions to any building or structure used in the veteran's business. The amount of such loans is limited to $25,000,000. The amount of the Government's guarantee is limited to 25 per cent of the loans made by a bank, if the total loans by that bank do not exceed $1,000,000. The guarantee is reduced to 15 per cent on the amount of loans made by each bank over $1,000,000. Records of loans made at March 31, 1947, are not yet available.
63.	Under the terms of The Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act, 1937, 125,720 loans had been made by banks and other approved loaning institutions to home owners under the terms of this Act and the total amount of such loans was $49,959,055. The Dominion's contingent liability arising out of these loans is limited to 15 per cent of the

aggregate of such loans made by approved lending institutions, but as the balance of these loans on December 31, 1946, was $59,335, the contingent liability of the Government is limited to this amount. Up to December 31, 1946, 1,277 loss claims for an aggregate amount of $463,996 had been paid. The ratio of total losses to total volume of loans, therefore, is only 0-93 of one per cent.
64.	Under the provisions of the Appropriation Act No. 5, 1942, the Home Extension Plan was started. It provided for loans, not exeeding in the aggregate $2,000,000, by banks under regulations similar to those of the Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act, for the purpose of financing the creation of additional self-contained housing units by alterations or additions to a building used solely or partially as a dwelling at the time of application for the loan. To March 31, 1946, fifty-nine loans for a total amount of $109,238 had been made. The Dominion's contingent liability arising out of these loans amounted to 15 per cent of the aggregate of such loans made by the banks of $16,386. There have been no claims for loss made by the -banks. Since March 31, 1946, no new loans have been made under this authority but under the authority of Part IV of the National Housing At, 1944.
65.	Part IV of the National Housing Act, 1944, authorizes loans to be made by chartered banks to home owners for improvement of their homes and for conversion of existing homes into multiple housing units, which loans may be guaranteed by the Government up to a maximum of $100,000,000. The contingent liability of the Government with respect to these loans is limited to 5 per cent of the aggregate of such loans made by each lending institution.
The home improvement loan section of the Act has not yet been proclaimed and therefore no loans have been granted thereunder. By Order in Council dated April 13, 1946, the home extension section of the Act was proclaimed. At March 31, 1947, twenty-eight loans had been approved in a total amount of $86,065 to provide for fifty-eight housing units. There have been no claims for losses. The contingent liability of the Government at March 31, 1947, was $4,303.
66.	Under the provisions of Part II, Section 11 (3A) of the National Housing Act, 1944, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation may guarantee -the principal of debentures of an institutional holding company and interest thereon at a rate of not more than two and one-half per cent per annum. At March 31, 1947, debentures had been issued

by Housing Enterprises of Canada Limited bearing -the guarantee of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the amount of $3,735,000.
67.	Under the Dominion Housing Act, 1935, the National Housing Act, 1938, and the National Housing Act, 1944, the Dominion has accepted and is accepting certain obligations arising out of its contracts with approved lending institutions which, while not expressed in the form of a guarantee, may nevertheless be regarded as contingent or indirect liabilities. On January 1, 1946, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, 1945, was proclaimed and since that date the Corporation has been acting as the agent of His Majesty in connection with loans under these Acts.
The manner in which losses in respect of any loan are -to be shared by the Dominion and the lending institution is fixed by the contract. The original principle under the Dominion Housing Act and the National Housing Act, -1938, was that the Dominion bears two-thirds of the loss, if at the time the loss is sustained the principal amount of the loan repaid, less any other amount due, is equal to or less than the amount advanced by the Dominion and one-third of the loss if at the time the loss is sustained the principal amount repaid, less any other amounts due, is more than the amount advanced by the Dominion. In the case of small loans (that is, loans not in excess of $4,000 in the case of single family dwellings or not in excess of $700 -per habitable room in the case of multiple family dwellings), the share of the loss to be -borne by the Dominion is not more than 80 per cent and not less than 50 per cent -of the loss. Under the National Housing Act, 1938, a new provision was added to encourage the making of small loans in small or remote communities and in districts or other communities designated by the Minister of Finance in any contract. In respect of such loans, the Dominion has -agreed in contracts with certain lending institutions to pay losses sustained by any such lending institution up to certain amounts determined by the contract which are not les3 than 7 per cent and do not exceed 25 per cent of the total amount of such loans made by each such lending institution. Under -the National Housing Act, 1944, -the Dominion bears the first one-quarter of the loss and agrees to pay losses sustained by any lending institution up to an amount set out in -the contract. This amount, by statute, cannot exceed 15 -per cent of the aggregate of the lending institution's share of the joint loans made by -the lending institution and His Majesty under the contract.

Mr. Speaker, it would be a very-ungenerous, churlish and indeed very foolish man, I think, who would seek to begin the speech that I am beginning in any other way than by congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on his first budget speech. Happily, under our system of government, we can do this with sincerity. I remember not long ago when, I think it was in the state of New York, the defeated candidate for the governorship congratulated the winner a friend of mine said, "I wonder what the Russians would think of that?" and his answer was, "I suppose they would regard it as deep-dyed hypocrisy". Mr. Speaker, I do congratulate the minister. I also understand the enthusiasm with which his budget has been received and I think, in large measure, we can all share his enthusiasm. Certainly I say, just as he has said, that it does justify pride and inspires confidence in this country. I do not for a minute hesitate to say that for, as lhe has very properly said, it is our budget. It is not his budget; it is the budget of everyone of us *throughout the country. His reference to Sir John Rose and the length of his speech prompted me to do a quick calculation, although it is not an accurate one. I have guessed that if the length of the minister's speech as compared with Rose's speech had been in proportion to the amounts involved, the minister's speech would have gone on for weeks; and, of course, if it had been in proportion to the surplus, about which I shall have something to say in a moment, perhaps the minister's speech would have gone on to infinity.
Having said these words, and with great sincerity, I wish to make some comments on the speech. Of course I intend to follow the practice on these occasions and speak for only a very few minutes. First, I wish to comment on this word "surplus." It strikes me as an unusual word. The minister spoke about it in the beginning; he spoke about it again at the end, and apparently with strong selfcongratulation; but he pointed out honestly that this $352,000,000 was not equal to the amount of the capital represented in the receipts, the special receipts of $372,000,000, which have nothing to do with income. I just want to point out to the minister that, as he is thoroughly aware, this is a strange habit we have in dealing with public accounts which, if it were practised in connection with private accounts, would result not only in the company going broke but probably in somebody having to go to jail. I would also suggest to the minister-and I know he will not

mind this-that years ago when he and I were both in private life and the company with which I was associated wished to seek- and gladly seek-advice from the firm with which he was associated, we never would have wanted approximate accuracy such as we have here. We never would have wanted anything just ninety per cent right, or eighty-five per cent right. I am sure he will agree that when we went to the very good firm with which he was associated we expected 100 per cent accuracy, and nothing less. I should like to point out that it ought to be easier for the government to gauge its expenditures than for the private corporation, because the government has control over so many of the elements entering into the matter.
I want to add just this one word. The minister should not ask us to be so grateful because he has taken several hundred million dollars of our money more than he needed to take, because, after all, that is what it amounts to. I would refer him to a speech made not so many years ago by a gentleman who will be received as a great authority by those immediately to my left, the Right Hon. Philip Snowden, who said that any chancellor of the exchequer who had even a half crown of surplus ought to be charged with getting money under false pretences.
I want to make just this final comment in that connection. We have drifted-and I see it again and again

into a state of affairs where governments really seem to have thought themselves into a state of mind whereby, when they come and announce a surplus, it is just as though they had presented to us a gift out of their own pockets. So often they seem to forget that this is our own money that has done these wonderful things. So I should just like to say that to me this does not seem like good budgeting but very bad budgeting. The government ought to be very much ashamed to come to us and tell us they are five or six hundred million dollars wrong. I really think the minister should have apologized to us for that tonight; and I believe there is an uncritical attitude abroad when people will thump their desks over that sort of thing. I am sure they will feel quite differently in the morning. Many people in this country wdll say to themselves, "Did they really get all this money they did not need? I could have done with that extra money of mine that they took away."

The minister is always apt, even when I do not hear him. In the few minutes which is all

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
I can allow myself 1 am not going to take time to comment on the way in which these reductions have been applied, but I should like to say two things. I listened to learn whether anything had been done for the unfortunate children who are still to be asked to pay for their chocolate bar and their pop an amount which apparently is beyond their resources. The minister's heart must have been wrung, I am sure, by a cartoon I and probably he read today, and I cannot understand why a man with such an open heart could have overlooked that point.
I wish to make one other comment of a much more serious nature, though that is serious enough. As far as I could judge on first hearing, it seemed to me there was no beginning to deal with the situation in regard to the gold industry which is so vital in that all important aspect of our business relations, namely, exchange with the United States.
I might deal with other matters, but I should like to say one word in regard to the excess profits tax. It seems to me a pity that it has to be continued on the present utterly unintelligible basis as to the basic period and standard rate.
There is one further comment I wish to make, and here I speak, I hope, with a sense of responsibility and a sense of moderation. In the minister's speech, which I noticed lasted for only two hours, not four hours like some other speeches-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: OTHER CANADIAN ECONOMIC STATISTICS MONTHLY FIGURES
speechtext: An hour and three-quarters.

maintopic: OTHER CANADIAN ECONOMIC STATISTICS MONTHLY FIGURES
speechtext:
The minister corrects me; he is more accurate than on some other occasions. During all that speech lasting an hour and three-quarters, according to the minister, only about five minutes were devoted to dominion-provincial relations. Indeed, his phraseology suggested that he might have left it out altogether. He began by saying, "Perhaps I should not let this occasion pass without a few comments about this important problem." I think we should be grateful that he did not let it pass altogether, but the comments he made were really proportionate in their importance to the length of time he took to make them. They were brief, and just related to us things we already knew. I wish to make a comment or two on that, because it seems to me that when we are invited to congratulate ourselves-as we may well do on the many favourable features we have seen-it is well to remind ourselves that here is a matter in which not only have we met failure but which, as a friend of mine put it to me the other day, is becoming a scandal; that responsible, sensible statesmen, speaking the same
language, thinking the same thoughts, with the same background, are not able to get together and sit sensibly around a table to discuss matters which are of great importance. We are inclined to criticize the failures that have been experienced at Moscow and elsewhere, but there they have had many difficulties we do not face. What has happened in the last year? On the money side we have had a kind of topsy-turvy, upside-down auction. The federal government has been the auctioneer, but it has been a strange kind of auction. They have bid up the various provinces, and the dominion, the auctioneer, has not received money, but has paid it. The dominion has paid money to everybody at the highest rate reached by anybody. So we have this perfectly topsy-turvy arrangement, which, as I say, has been brought about by this individual method of auction in reverse. Even then we should remember that nobody understands what we have done, because there is an area of uncertainty on the fringe of the whole business. Nobody knows just what has been decided; nobody knows what is to be left to the provinces and what to the dominion. The minister himself was very frank about the matter when speaking in Toronto some weeks ago.
I should like to make this final comment. It seems to me that this is a matter which goes to the very root of our national life. All these pleasant things we have been hearing tonight-and many of them are pleasant- can turn sour and have little effect if we are not able to get together as men of good will and talk these things out. As I was considering what the minister said tonight I pictured to myself the table in the senate chamber. Actually a year ago today, I believe, they were seated there, the Prime Minister at the head, as was fitting, with the premiers of the different provinces. I was thinking that if that meeting took place now there would be three absentees. Why would there be three absentees? Who are these men who apparently are not considered proper to be dealt with? These are men in high standing in their own provinces, one of them formerly a minister here, all of them returned to power more than once in their own provinces. Why is it that we cannot have this? Why is it that we stand as we do now? Is it because of the old maxim which I presume the Prime Minister learned at the university as many of us did-divide and conquer? Can it be that? Is that the reason, or can it be that there is some other reason? Whatever the reason may be, I, who am a newcomer here, make this suggestion, with respect, to the Prime Minister:	Our ancestors had old-
Emergency Powers

fashioned ways of talking about it and they might have said, "Will not the Prime Minister as a thank-offering for the return of his health -which we all so greatly rejoice over-now that he is back-say that this thing will be changed, that we shall now try to get together and reconfederate this country which is in such great, need of reconfederation and reintroduce the spirit which existed in this country eighty years ago?"-as the Minister of Finance so well expressed it tonight. I put that forward with deference but with earnestness, and I move that this debate be now adjourned.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish
to continue what I was saying when the committee rose at six o'clock. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply interrupted me as I was about to conclude my remarks. I had just referred to the laying of hardwood flooring at the rate of three cents per square foot.
I want to tell the minister that between the time the committee rose at six o'clock and the house met at eight o'clock I telephoned no fewer than nine different flooring firms in Ottawa, and on no occasion did I get a bid anywhere near three cents. Not one of them would accept floor laying at the rate of three cents per square foot. I wanted to put this on the record to show that I was not very far out when I made the statement the other day that fair wages could be made at five cents per square foot. I think a man could make fair wages at that rate, but certainly not at three cents.
The thing I was more concerned about was the increase in the prices of retail lumber. It would be a very bad thing for this country and especially for the building industry and those people with small incomes who are endeavouring to get better homes, our returned men particularly. It will be a great impediment to them if prices of retail lumber are allowed to go up. I pointed out before the dinner recess, and I think it is worth mentioning again, that the minister should take some precautions in this regard.

It was brought to my attention during the Easter recess that a great many retail lumber yards are selling grades Nos. 2 and 3 for No. 1 prices. That is something which the minister should talk over with his different controllers and have investigated. It is not reasonable and it will not lead to good construction.
More consideration should be given to increasing production, and I am glad to hear the minister say that a greater percentage of our cut is to be kept at home rather than exported. When we were speaking on this matter during last session I mentioned that there was far too much of our lumber, particularly the better grades, being exported instead of being kept at home to meet the needs of the people of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I would not have spoken except that the hon. member for Comox-Albemi made some disparaging remarks about this group. He insinuated that we believe that anybody who was not on relief was an enemy of the state. I think the significance to be attached to his remarks lies in the fact that they received intense applause also from the Tory representatives on the right. The true alliance with regard to such matters is certainly evident when so many members applaud the manner in which big business exercises complete control over the life of the people of this country.
I think the reference he was making to our group had probably to do with our reference to the greatest lumber king in the world today. I am not attacking this man personally, but I just want to give the details of the kind of thing that we object to through the abuse of great powers by such persons. This man has operated under a system which he has exploited to the full. It is to such exploitation of our natural resources that we object. I spent some time looking up "Who's Who in Canada", a book in the library which gave me an outline of the kind of thing that this man was able to do.
He started off in 1911 as assistant director of the forestry branch of the old Department of the Interior, Ottawa. He discovered where Canada's forest resources lay. In 1912 he got himself appointed, through some political pull, I suppose, chief forester of the province of British Columbia, which is noted for its vast forest wealth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps through his ability.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps through his ability, yes. In that position he made a survey of the timber resources of that province. He came back to Ottawa in 1915 as special

Emergency Powers
timber trade commissioner and he made a
trip around the world and visited practically every continent. This was a most important trip for him in view of me fact that later on he went into business for himself and through large shipping firms exported lumber to those very countries.
In 1916 and 1917 he was sales manager for the Victoria Lumber Manufacturing Company. From 1917 to 1919 he came back as assistant director of the imperial munitions board. Then a most significant thing happened after the war. He went back to British Columbia and he framed the timber royalty act of that province. Remember you are dealing with natural resources which belong to all the people. We believe that these resources are the birthright of the Canadian people and that they should be developed for their use and not be given away so that one individual can make tremendous profits for himself. We believe that if the Canadian people need lumber with which to build houses they should be able to get that lumber to build houses and that no individual should be given power over these resources to export them to the markets of the world and make himself a multi-millionaire. I understand that this firm paid $400 million for timber rights on Vancouver Island, the leases of which had been formerly held by John D. Rockefeller, Junior. He started to expand from then on until his ships sailed the seven seas to every continent of the world. He became head of his own export company, president of British Columbia Packers, president of Alberni Plywoods, president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, a director of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, a director of the Dominion Power and Chemical Company, a director of Forest Investment Company and of International Nickel, president of London and Western Trusts, president of British Columbia Plywoods, president of the Canadian Transport Company, president of the Canadian White Pine Company, president of the Alberni Pacific Transport Company and a member of the Canadian advisory board of the Sun Life Assurance Company.
With his knowledge of lumber he performed valuable service to this government as timber controller in 1940, and later as chairman of the wartime requirements board. After apparently some misunderstanding with the minister, he was later made president of wartime merchant shipping and, I believe, gave valuable service to Canada in his capacity as a manager in building ships for Canada.
We in this group do not consider, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni insinuated, that just because a man has amassed wealth he is 83166-167
therefore an enemy of the state. But we do believe that the resources of this country should not be available to any person to develop to make himself a multi-millionaire and deny in the development of those resources the very things that are essential to the Canadian people in building houses. Housing is more than a roof over one's head. It has sociological values. Bad housing is a cause of crime. But these people have taken the natural resources which belong to the Canadian people and exploited them to their own advantage. They were not thinking of the Canadian people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would ask the minister how priorities are arranged and what quotas timber producers in British Columbia are allowed to export. How do you arrive at the portion of their cut which they are permitted to export? Is it on a quota basis? Is it given to those people who have the facilities for export and have contacts in other countries? What is done about the little fellow who is doing a small timber cutting job on the side of a mountain where perhaps there is not a vast forest?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The answer is very simple. The little man has exactly the same chance to export as the big man. He is entitled to export sixty per cent of his total cut, provided that he places the other forty per cent on the market. I think practically all timber men big and small, take advantage of their export cut. The figures would seem to indicate that.
I should like to say a few words about the speech made tonight by the hon. member for Yorkton, because it was indicative of the attitude of the group to which my hon. friend belongs. He sees nothing in the career of H. R. MacMillan except that he has made money for himself. But that was purely

Emergency Powers

incidental. Two of the greatest builders that this country ever saw died bankrupt, but they left a great trail in this country. I refer to Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann. Trace the careers of these two men across the country and you will see the great contribution they made to the wealth of the country today. You will see the same in H. R. MacMillan. There was no great timber industry in British Columbia when he started his operations there. He has contributed greatly to the wealth of British Columbia and to the well-being of its people, and he has contributed to the wealth of Canada by creating markets abroad for its natural resources. When my hon. friend says that Mr. MacMillan has done nothing to replace those forests, he is totally ignorant on that point. Anyone who speaks on the subject should take the opportunity to inform himself to some extent. I sincerely hope that a man of his age will take a little broader view of this dominion of ours and of what makes it grow, and give some credit to men who have shown the energy and the resourcefulness of the man to whom he referred and speak of them with some respect.

speechtext: The reference I made was to the fact that the Canadian people are short of lumber and that if this lumber is used it should be used for the benefit of the Canadian people more than for the benefit of one particular individual who has apparently worked his way up under the system under which we live. I do not think it is fair for hon. members to make personal remarks across the floor. Some of the argument that took place here this afternoon may have been unfortunate. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni made a slighting remark to the hon. member for Yorkton. I believe the remark was that, had the hon. member for Yorkton as much ambition as somebody else who was taking part in the discussion at that time, he might have been a better man. May I say a word about these next two orders P.C. 1665 and P.C. 469? Actually they were passed in the committee on Thursday last. I have drawn to the atten-
Emergency Powers

tion of the minister a clause in these two orders which does not fit the facts, and I would ask leave of the committee to reopen these two orders for the purpose of introducing correcting amendments which the minister has in hand.
May I just in a word mention the point involved in the two orders? These are orders dealing with the administration of property of persons of the Japanese race by the custodian of enemy property. Section 3 of the first order, P.C. 1665, reads as follows:
For the purposes of the control and management of such property hy the custodian, the consolidated regulations respecting trading with the enemy (1939), shall apply mutatis mutandis to the same extent as if the property belonged to an enemy within the meaning of the said consolidated regulations (as amended by P.C. 2483, March 27, 1942).
A. similar provision appears in order P.C. 469:
. . . and for the purpose of such liquidation, sale or other disposition the consolidated regulations respecting trading with the enemy (1939) shall apply mutatis mutandis as if the property belonged to an enemy within the meaning of the said consolidated regulations.
Actually these consolidated regulations of 1939 were superseded completely by new regulations in 1943, many of which were revoked in January of this year. It will be necessary to make changes in the wording to take account of the changes made in the consolidated regulations. I have discussed this matter with the minister, Mr. Chairman, and I believe he has an amendment prepared along these lines.

speechtext: I wish to say a few words on this order in council. There are two orders in council, P.C. 133/510 and P.C. 3396, dealing with merchant seamen, and I take it that we can discuss them both at the same time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does the committee agree? The committee agrees to discuss both orders in council at the same time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
At this late hour it would perhaps not be right to make any extensive remarks, but we all recognize the great importance of the merchant seamen and the magnificent service they gave during the war. They were called, I believe, the fourth branch of the service, and, rightly so. It is pretty hard to estimate just what the people of the country owe to these men, but we get some idea when we realize that there were over 1,200 casualties among the merchant seamen during the war-over 600 fatal casualties. As a matter of fact, it has been estimated that the casualties were heavier among the merchant seamen than they were in any other branch of the services for the numbers engaged1 ir that work. Of 185,000 men engaged in the merchant marine of Great Britain, there were 38,000 fatal casualties. I say this in order to give some idea of the great risk, and the great sacrifice which was made by these men.
Enlistments in the merchant marine were, as we know, of young men and old men. Many of them were young men who had been turned down for service in the other branches, and the others were older men who were too old to serve in those branches. In our veterans affairs committee last year the services of these men were partly recognized, in that they were included in the Pension Act for disabilities during their service. However we understood then-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, and I would be the last to attempt to stop him from discussing benefits or establishments of any kind to which merchant seamen are entitled. But I understand, from the ruling of the Chairman,

Emergency Powers
already given, that the discussion should be centred around one or the other of these orders in council. The first one has to do with compensation for merchant seamen, for the loss of their effects; the other has reference to out-of-work benefits, and I presume my hon. friend wants to discuss benefits other than those to which merchant seamen might be entitled. My suggestion is that that is not in order.
Mr. BROOKS; I was discussing out-of-work benefits. There is one thing we have recognized, I believe, through all these orders in council, namely, that we have not been confined to the absolute wording of the order in council. There has been considerable leeway, and I contend that in discussing benefits in connection with the merchant seamen, and out-of-work allowances, we can give expression to what we consider are benefits that should have been extended to these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: This is clearly out of order. My hon. friend must realize that he is talking about a different kind of benefit entirely. He is apparently going to advocate gratuities or something like that, which would come under veterans legislation or civil service legislation, whereas we are talking about compensation to seamen, war damage to their effects, and that does not open the door to a broad discussion of the problems of merchant seamen. If we do not get down to business some time this session we shall never get anywhere.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

Under P.C. 133/510 this is for compensation to fishermen and personnel of the Canadian merchant navy for loss of effects during enemy action or counter action. Section 8 at page 159 of the office consolidation of the orders in council states that until the appropriate department otherwise directs, no compensation shall be payable under these regulations in respect of any claim which has not been made within one year after a war damage has been incurred. The date of this first regulation was in 1944, and there were manj' merchant seamen who had suffered damage and who lost their effects before that year. I should like to know from the minister just what if anything has been done to compensate these men for the loss of their equipment before that date, and why it says a year from the date of loss. I know that when we were discussing this matter in the veterans affairs committee it was considered that these men might perhaps be away from home for long periods and that it would be impossible for them to enter their claim. In view of the fact that this order in council was passed in 1944. would any provision be made for these many thousands of men who lost their equipment and personal effects through enemy action prior to that date?
Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to contribute a few remarks to the discussion of these orders in council, especially P.C, 4306 dealing with the shortage of trained personnel in the merchant marine, and therefore the sending out of ships under circumstances where their trained personnel are not as qualified as they normally would be; and also with P.C. 3396, which deals with unemployment benefits to seamen, which are benefits, of course, mainly to non-technical personnel. The lack of a proper Canadian merchant marine in the past causes the shortage of trained personnel at the present time. The out-of-work and unemployment benefits are a direct result of large numbers entering the merchant marine during the war, of course through necessity; and now, because of the policy of the government of disbanding that merchant marine which we built up during the war we find that we have large numbers of sailors on the beach. I have had communications from the marine council of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada and also from the seafarers international union of North America complaining of this fact. For example, the trend at the present time is to sell the whole of what was formerly the Canadian merchant marine to foreign interests; whether it be to British interests or others, it does not matter. In fact, they could be sold to Canadian interests. But what is happening is that the ships are being put under Panamanian registry, a country which has no maritime laws. Therefore crews can be hired under any conditions whatsoever and our Canadian seamen can be left on the beach. That is what is happening at the present time. What the seamen are interested in at the moment is this: Is the government going to bring down amendments to the Canada Shipping Act at the present time, and is the government going to stop the importation of foreign crews to man boats going out of Vancouver?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The fact that these orders in council are put through shows that there is a shortage of trained technical personnel. If there was a decent merchant marine policy, you would not have these orders in council. Granted you would have the unemployment benefits, but they' wtould not be needed with the heavy amount of shipping that is going out of our ports at the present time if we had a Canadian merchant marine. Are we to be faced once again with a crisis where we have to call in experts of foreign nations to take over the job of officering our ships in another crisis? That is what will happen owing to the lack of foresight of the government at the present time unless something is done.. I should be pleased now to hear if the government is considering bringing down amendments to the Canada Shipping Act at the present time, to protect seamen from this policy.
Let me give an illustration of what is happening. A ship will be taken out of the port of Seattle and towed up to the port of Vancouver to be overhauled. It will be manned with a United States crew to bring it up to Vancouver. Then a Chinese crew will be imported to put on board that ship in the port of Vancouver, because that cannot be done in Seattle. Canadian seamen are thinking of picketing these ships. You are going to have labour trouble about this. Can we expect any help from the government in protecting our Canadian seamen on jobs which should be their own?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I fail to see how the question which my hon. friend asks has anything to do with any of the orders in council which are under discussion. However, in case he may think that I do not want to answer the questions which he asks, I may tell him that amendments to the Canada Shipping Act are matters which cannot be disposed of in a short time. There are some eight hundred sections to the Canada Shipping Act. In my estimation not only one but many amendments are required. I have asked a group of

Emergency Powers
officers of my department to look into the question of amending the act. So far as I ean see at the moment, I do not think it will be possible to bring down amendments to the Canada Shipping Act at this session. However I hope that at the next session of parliament it will be possible to make amendments to the act which will perhaps not meet the situation which my hon. friend speaks of but which will have in mind a- number of complaints which have been made against the operation of that act, and to make a number of amendments which I think are justified.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to thank the minister for his answrer, because any improvement in the present situation will be beneficial. I recognize that it takes time to overhaul this act. In fact, when it was put through in 1934 the present Minister of Veterans Affairs and the present Minister of Labour objected to the speedy way in which this was done. I am glad that the department is taking plenty of time to go over it. I hope that it will bear with the representations made by labour and put in many of the points which labour is asking for at the present time, and which are incorporated in the laws of many of the modern seagoing nations.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the minister himself prepared to insert those words in this particular clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

This process here, I am told, is not directly connected with drilling.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to point out to the minister that this is not a refining process. This particular piece of apparatus might really be considered as an extension to the piece of pipe which brings the oil up from the ground. The apparatus simply separates from that oil the sand and water found in it, enabling the oil to be shipped, particularly in the winter time. As I understand it, if this oil is put in tanks to be shipped during cold weather there is a freezing of the water contained in the oil, and consequently there is great difficulty in getting the oil out of the railway tank cars or other containers, with the likelihood of damage. As a result, the oil cannot be made use of in the winter time particularly, unless it is treated in this manner. So I do not think this should be looked upon as a refining process.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

This apparatus has nothing at all to do with the well but is apparatus for taking the water out of the oil after it leaves the well.

speechtext:
There is one matter I
should like to speak to, and I can do so in the space of two minutes if I may proceed now. It is in relation to the schedule generally. AVe have just completed a review of a schedule which embodies 163 pages of fine print; yet if the bill is enacted in its present form, or with the schedule in its present form, it will appear as a bill about four pages in length. I submit that the schedule to the bill should contain the text in full of the orders as amended which are now to receive statutory effect. All that we have in the present schedule is a reference to these orders by number, date and name. I submit that the text of the orders ought to appear in the schedule to the bill itself.
My reasons are briefly these: First of all, there must be an official text of these orders which now receive the force and effect of statute. At present that is not to be found in the statute itself; one must refer to the original orders which are on file in the privy council office. I submit that that is not the proper form in which this parliament should legislate.
In the second place, there is a distinct gap in the statute books. People who wish to know the statute law of this country are entitled to find it in the statute books, and they will not be able to do so if this schedule is passed in its present form. Here is a whole volume which will be missing from the statute books if the schedule does not contain the full text of the orders. It may be that power is reserved to revoke certain orders, but I submit that when these orders become the statute law of the land they should appear in full in the schedule. Therefore, without further elaboration of the point, which I suggest is self-evident, I move:
That the schedule to Bill No. 104 as amended be further amended by printing therein the text in full of the orders in council numbered in the first column, as amended by those numbered in the fourth column in the said schedule.
